div.p: eariettes.
Extract from young lady's letter to friend staying at Yenice :—" Last night Flay in a gondola on the grand canal drinking it all in. Life never seemed so full _ _

before." An old man of our acquaintance says he was born at the wrong time. "When I was young,' he says, "young men were of no account; and now that I am old, old men are of no account." "Do you call that a veal cutlet, waiter ?" said an ex- quisite. " Why, sir, such a veal cutlet as that is an in- sult to every self-respecting calf in the British Empire!" The waiter hung his head in very shame for a moment, and then replied in the language of humblest apology: "I really didn't intend to insult you, sir." Two young men, East-enders, thee Musical Times tells us, strayed into St. Paul's Cathedral; one afternoon and became very interested. At one 'lean of the anthem where a quiet " verse" succeeded loud chorus, the sud- denness of the contrast so moved one of them that he turned with an anxious face to his companion and said, "Did you 'ear that? Pretty near a breakdown that time, 'Arry, wasn't it ?" A father complained bitterly of the way his children destroyed their clothing. eille said: "When I was a boy I had only one suit of clothes, and I had to take care of it. I was only allowed one pair of shoes in those days." There was a pause, and then the eldest boy 'spoke up and said: "I say, dad, you have a much easier time of it now you are living with usi." An anecdote was told me the other day, which, being true, is worth repeating. The late Duke of Rutland, when walking one fine morning in his grounds, came across a gamekeeper's little girl. "Well, little one," he asked, "and what do you call yourself ?" "For what we are going to receive, may the Lord make us truly thankful." replied the little one, with apparent irrele- vance. It seemed that the child's mother's instructions had been, "If you meet the duke, be quite sure to say your Grace.'" Sergeant Robinson records one of the wittiest sayings which have yet been ascribed to Lord Westbury. EilS lordship, although always professing to be a staunch Churchman, was not a very reviler attendant at church. On beim, chareed with inconsistency by a friend, who told him that be was bound to sepport his theory by his example, Lord Westbury replied, "I dare say you are right; but I am like one of the buttresses of the edifice, which are of much more service to it on the outside than the in." CURIOUS CHRIS/WM! Cusroms.—The natives of New Mexico are half-civilised, and from the fact of their living in pueblo., or village., are called the Pueblo Indians. They are mostly Christians, and as such, they observe Christmas Day. On this festive day they have one curious custom which is partly heathen in its origin. They then lay on the altar little char images of horses, sheep, cows, deer, and so forth. it seems that this means that they have beer: successful farmers or hunters durine the year, and that they have had a particular amount of success in rearing or chasing the animal whose image is thus placed on the altar on Christmas Day at the feet of the Great Spirit. A traveller who had entered one of their churches on this day was astounded to hear the warbling of birds—the thrush and canary especially—throughout the building. Making his way to the gallery whence the songs appeared chiefly to come, he ,fI,CV some 20 boys lying on the floor, each with a basin of water before him. and blowing into it through a reed split in such a way as to imitate the notes of various birds. This was the band of music for the fes- tival. Outside of the church and in the village square the Indians were dancing to the sound of a drum, and the droving was kept up during the three following days.— Little Folks' Magazine. A LVING Rome—A number of boys were skating and slidine in Yorkshire nearly a hundred years ago. On a sudden the ice gave way ahnest in the middle of the lake, and:one poor fellow fell in. There was no house near where they cud run fore help ; no ropes which tliey could throw to their struggling companion. Th boys stoo I on the bank, with pale sorrowful faces, afraid to try to reach their friend, in case the ice should give way, and swallow them all up. But one boy suddenly remembered that although you cannot stand a board upright on thin ice without its going through, yet if you Jay the same board flat on the ice it will be quite safe. Not only that., but he knew that he could run along the board without fear of cracking the ice. It only took him a moment to remember all that; the next he spoke to his friends something after this fashion—" I will lie down flat on the ice near the edge; then one of you must c.tme to my feet and push me along till you too can lie down. If you all lie down in that way, and push the boy in front of you, we shall make a line long enough to roach poor Reuben." Thus, taking the post of dan- ger him•elf, the brave boy was able by his living rope to reach his friend, He pulled him out, though he was not one moment too soon, for he was so exhausted with his efforts to keep his head above water that he would very soon have sunk.—Little Folks' Magazine. A CONGENIAL HOME.—sow that the days are shorter and the winter evenings upon us, let us invent ways and means by which we can make our homes compete successfully with the numerous enticing places of enter- tainment held open wherever men and boys are wont to oongregate—not because they naturally love drink and loose company, but pecauee there is that implanted in our nature which domends brightness and entertain- ment, and if that is net furni-hed at home they will seek it wherever it is to be found, regardless of character. Mothers who have sons to rat, and who fear the debas- ing influence of immoral associates, should study the nature of young manhood; its excessive restlessness; its disturbine, vain ambit Vele ; its thirst for action and longing for excitement; its irrepressible desire to be- come acquainted with the world and its ways. Build bright fires by night till the parent countenance shines with a brightness that lights up everything and every- one who comes within its influence. Hang pretty pictures on its walls, and fill the tables and booksneives with good books and entertaining papers. Permit and encourage innocent and lively games. Banish all skeletons from be- hind the doors, and the demons of dulness and apathy that may have hitherto ruled the household, and bring in their stfad mirth and cheerfulness. Stimulate and encourage the ambitions of the children in worthy direc- tions. If sons do not turn out well, blame it on the mis- directed influence of parents and home, for it is possible by right means and, exertion for a mother to have more control over the destiny of her boys and girls than any other influence. Some CONUNDRUMS.—" Why is an old dog like a rail- way gradient ?" "Because he is a slope un !" Perhaps, as this is our first, we ought to add that we mean "he is a slow pup !" And this leads to another, "Why are old cabbaees carried through Chiswick ?" " Because it's the way to Turnheen Green." "Why is a short nearo like a white man ?" "Because he's not at all black." eoWhen does a boy have a vegetable timekeeper ?" "When he has a turnip !" "No ; when he gets a notate clock;" which, it may be as well to explain, requires to be understood as up at eight o'clock." "Why Ps killing bees litre confessing? "Because you unbuzz'em." "Why is a mouse-trap so cowardly ?" "Because it is such a puzzle-any-mouse affair," which, please to note, is to be further understood as a "pusillanimous" affair. "Wiry are the Hadeudowas like a process of reason- ing ?" "Because they are a racy bossy nation." "When is a herring like a tired horse " When it is hard rode." " What is the difference between Noah's Ark and an Archleishop ?" "One was a high ark, and the other is a hierarch!" This seems old; quite archaeological, in fact. Some of its predecessors seem familiar; but then it is • not easy to make a new pun, and when we are dealing in conundrums we really cannot atop to inquire as to who holds the copyright. "Why is photography antagonistic to portrait painting ?" "Because it is mm pho-toeraphic art. "What wig cannot be made by a barber?" "An earwig." "Why are there no eggs in Hayti ?" "Because the negroes extirpated the whites and threw off their yolk !'"' What fish would you send to wake up a John Dory ?" "A sturgeon." "Finally, for we are getting tired of this attenuated humour. "What monkeys make the best wine?" "Why, gray apes to be sure !' DRUNREWMSS CURED.—A Wealthy Ameritan Lady whose Only son for years was a slave to Intemperance, Nervous Depression and Exhausted Vitality, after seeking in vain for a cure, and trying all known remedies, at last found a simple means that cured and saved him from a drunkard's grave. Anyone suffering or desiring to help others in this worthy eause, by sending a tell-addressed stamped envelope to Mr. James Holland, 25, Hart-st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information, free of charge. div.head: LOOKING FORWARD
div.p: LOOKING FORWARD
BY H. WHITIIAM.

Your readers will perhaps remember the interest- ing lecture delivered in the Co-operative Hall by the Rev. W. Tuckwell entitled "The New Utopia, or England in 1985." In it the rev, gentleman sketched a state of society in which "no one was permitted to be idle, no one might work less than six nor more than nine hours in the day.' This, a quotation from More's Utopia, written nearly 400 years ago, contains the underlying principle of i what s termed the highest principle, "the love and service of others," the people's highest aim, bodily health, long life, beauty, mental enjoyment, knowledge and self-improvement." Strange that, in a book written so long ago, the writer should, as Mr. Tuckwell observes, have put his linger on the very sores from which the body social of our day is ailing. I must ask your readers to hear with me a little, if I, Cassandra like, wander off a little in this letter and strike against a few of the rocks ahead. It is just two years agn, since me and mine packed up bag and baggage, acid left your dear old town. What our feelings were I could scarcely tell, or what we expected to find in this far away land of the Golden West. Of one thing lat all events was certain, and that was, that there was room enough, not only for ma and mine. but for the many thou- ' sands who were for ever leaving the shores of Great Britain behind them. It may be, aud I know will be said," Ati well, the fact is, ho hadn't energy enough in him; he was wanting in that aptitude which enables a man to gain a position in the world." This may be all true, but it in no wise affects the fact that out here there are thousands upon thou- sands of Englishmen who felt themselves crowded out, and in sheer desperation determined to seek "fresh woods and pastures new." Is it possible to find out the cause of the misery, and the sharp anxiety which exists in so many English homes? I think it is : but as I intend to deal with matters on this side the Atlantic, your readers must please un- ravel the argument for themselves when I have done.

div.head: POVERTY AND WEALTH.
div.p: POVERTY AND WEALTH.

I have just -reCeived the Labour Commissioners' report, and I find that England is not the only place in which the workman finds the struggle for a mere existence a very keen' one. In New York the wretched story of "Outcast London "is repeated ; women are making shirts at twenty cents the dozen, working hard all day, and wearily plodding the streets at night. All through the States men are amassing such fortunes as altogether baffle the com- prehension. To be the owner of a million sterling (or five million dollars) don't count for much. The only wealthy men are they who are burdened with fortunes of twenty and thirty million dollars. It is the possibility of these immense fortunes accumu- lating in the hands of one man that is now creating a most powerful and surprising amount of excite- ment. Added to this, the growth of trusts, syndi- cates, and other huge coipbinations of wealth has caused the well-to-do to be stirred, and aroused to the great necessity of at once bestirring themselves if the country is to be saved from what might prove to be a sangtunary revolution. Socialism has, as we know, been making itself heard throughout Europe. In England its growth has, in the larger cities, been steady and persistent, and is only to be attributed to a feeling of uneasiness on the part of wage earners, whip, finding themselves in daily competi- tion with their fellow workers, live in constant dread as to where to-morrow's bread and butter are to come from. On this side the Atlantic THE LABOUR QUESTION is looming up as the great rock ahead against which the Ship of State may 'at any time crash. Here, as in. England, it is a usual sight to see scores of men waiting at the factory gates seeking employment —men ieared in the lowest grades of civilization, Hungarians, Mexicans, Italians, Germans, and Scandinavian peasants, knowing nothing of the English language, having no knowledge of European and American artizan workmen's higheraspiratior s ; and as a consequence these men are at the mercy of unprincipled employers, taking such wages as they can get, and herding together after their own primitive fashion. This, coupled with the still more fearful Chinese question, makes the labour problem a difficult one to solve.

div.head: TRADE UNIONISM
div.p: TRADE UNIONISM

is powerful; but, I fear, unable to cope with the question. It proceeds too much on the old lines. Instead of seeking to make the workman master of the sourced of wealth,and of the tools of industry, it depends upon arbitrary repressiln of grievances; destruction, and not construction. But this is a new country; I mean more especially this side the Rockies. Workmen, as a rule, are not acquainted with the history of English Trade Unionism, and have therefore much to learn, and I am very pleased to say are willing to learn. My Trades Unionism is not of a very combative kind. This is well known in Warrington, I think. Being a thorough Evolutionist. I believe in grad aal growth. The unprincipled employer I would sweep out of my path remorselessly, but with the employer generally I must always ask myself, "What would Ido were lin his place ?" Evolution teaches a gradual and certain change in the circumstances and environments of society. have alluded to a surprising amount of excitement which now exists throughout the States on the question of boundless wealth on the one hand, and the most abject povety on the other hand. The ideals of Mcre, and more recently of Mr. Tuckwell, and other writers, seem to have culminated in Bellamy's "LOOKING BACKWARD."

Nationalist clubs are springing up in all direc- tions, and it is sought to bring about, as soon as may be, the perfect state which the hero of " Look- ing Backward" finds when he wakes from his mesmeric sleep of a century. lie finds Boston a bigger, brighter, and even brainier city than ever. But the social conditions are entirely changed. The Government has become the employer of all —the provider of all. Service is required of all between the ages of 21 and 45. After that the income of each continues, but each may pass his time as he chooses. Machinery has become so efficient that the hours of those who labour are but brief. There is no money and no wages. In place of this persons receive& non-transferable certificate, entitling them to 'an equal share in the annual product of the country. For convenience sake this is made up in book form, with little coupons represent- ing dollars anj cents, and when the holder makes a purchase the amount is punched out. There are no prisons and no poorhouses. Neither are there any churches; every one is con- nected with the "sermon room" by telephone. So with the lecture-rooms and concert-halls. Like the Theosophists

AMERICAN NATIONALISTS declare the principle of the Brotherhood of Humanity to be one of the eternal truths that govern the world's progress; and aim at des- troying competition, declaring that so long as it continues to be the ruling factor in our industrial system, the highest development of the individual cannot be reached. They seek to push the prin- ciple which underlies the syndicate system a little further, and have all industries operated in the interest of all by the nation. A peculiar feature in the movement is that the working classes, as yet, take no interest in it, and for this they get well abused. The dame and I attended a meeting the other evening which was indeed half a concert, and I made a special point of trying to find out 'how

many working-men were present. At my own Club the following evening, I was forced to acknowledge that the horny-handed one was conspicuous only by his absence. The Nationalists declare that reformers, hitherto, have looked too much to the ignorant classes,' meaning by that the working- men, and are now determined to look higher; they are assured that—

The Icing of fools Finds his readiest tools, In the ranks of the working classes. Since the days of Robert Owen, Europe has seen numerous efforts made to establish these ideal societies. From various causes these have failed ; but, it is now contended that things are ripe and success must attend this new movement. Being a firm believer in
TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANU

div.head: Co-OPERATION
div.p: Co-OPERATION

without the " divi," I have of eourse laid the sys- tem, which is quite new here, before them; and with such success that I have to occupy the floor and deal with the subject exhawstively. I think I see, in spite of Cassandra, a migiktv and most won- derful change coming over the people of tbe whole industrial world. In fact, not only the masses, but the classes, are bestirring themselves. Christianity is waking up, and if your readers will turn to the "Christian World" of September 19th they will there find it recorded that " a new spirit was abroad. The aristocracy ;of the people—the aristo- cracy of labour, benevolence, and humanity—was coming forward to take the place of the aristo- cracy of laziness, and luxury." Yes, new social and intellectual problems are coming to the front, and these will demand no half-way answers. The great strike you have had in London has roused the world, and it is felt here that such an occurrence, ,if not of the same magnitude, yet equal in its social effects, may not be far from our own doors. I see Dr. Clifford, speaking in London, advocated "some emigration scheme." I beg that Englishmen will not look to the 'States as an outlet. As a mem- ber of the Labour Council of the Pacific slope I have great opportunities for learning the state of

div.head: _TIE_ LABOUR MARKET,
div.p: _TIE_ LABOUR MARKET,

and I state definitely and truthfully i-,hat it is over- crowded, Not a factory in the city but has crowds of men around the gates of a morning seeking jobs. As chairman of Labour Organization, I hnd a general dread amongst workmen of giving offence to employers lest situations should be lost, the men not knowing where to turn their faces for fresh work. I am bound to say that there is a patriotic feeling amongst employers to keep wages up, and to keep a high standard of living amongst the people; but everyone knows that the employer, as well as the employee, haste bend before competition. There are thousands of acres of land here waiting for the plough, but there are thousan4s of reasons why Englishmen should be careful before leaving the old land to take hold of these plough stilts. I should fancy all, or nearly all, eligible sites are already in the hands of speculators Irrigation has to be con- sidered; railway convenience does not count for much when it is known that California is three times as large as the State of New York, and much larger than Italy. Going to live en a new ranch is some- thing fearful, and only the hardest and roughest natures can come out of such camping out work successfully. Now, -whit have we to look forward to? Let your readers look at the recent speech of Lord Derby, at Rochdale. His remarks on Co-opera- tion are to the point, and contliin the answer to the whole puzzle. Distributive Co-operation has proved a success ; push it further still, and

div.head: PRODUCTIVE CO-OPERATION
div.p: PRODUCTIVE CO-OPERATION

will also be a success. It will solve the eight hours que.stion, the population question and the poverty question. Since writing the alsOve I have spoken several times on Co-operation, and I find it is con- founded with the various communistic movements to which I have alluded, and which have failed.l Recent articles in the ' New Review,' and in the Forum,' have helped immensely to throw light on the matter, and now 1 think that a great effort will be made in tlfls city to teach the people true Co- operation, and so had on to a Nationalism which will not be confiscation, and will imperceptibly replace IndividualisT by a humane spirit of emula- tion such as will satMfy all who hope to bring about peace en earth, and good-will towarck all men. May I say to all our friends that we are all well in health ; trade witn us is good, and we are looking forward to a happy Christmas; and to our friends at home we wish them a happy Christmas, and with the New Year increasing prosperity. 810, Bay-st., San Francisco, Dec. 6th, 1889.

div.head: – REPORTED GREAT NIHILIST PLOT.
div.p: - REPORTED GREAT NIHILIST PLOT.

The• Paris " Dixneuvietne Steele" announces that an extensive Nihilist plot against the Czar has been dis- covered at St. Petersburg, add that several of the con- spirators had actually made their way into the Imperial Palace. They were arrested in the lobbies and pas- sages, where one of them was killed by an officer of the Czar's household.

div.head: EVICTIONS AT TIPPERARY.
div.p: EVICTIONS AT TIPPERARY.

The evictions of Mr. Smith-Barry's Tipperary tenants was resumed on Monday. The sub-sheriff was protected by sixty policemen, under Colonel Caddell. Three shop- keepers and fifteen labourers, with their families, were evicted. Dr. Morrissy certified that the wife of one of the shopkeepers, James Carew, was unfit to be removed, as she was confined to bed suffering from paralysis. The sheriff agreed not to disturb her, but, her friends after- wards removing her, the eviction was completed.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.

Early on Saturday morning,a Kendal postman, named John Johnstown, made a soniewhat serious attack with a hatchet, upon his wife, who was suffering from inflam- mation of the lungs, and afterwards committed suicide on the railway, by placing himself on the rails. When found, his head was almost severed from his body. At the inquest, in the afternoon, it was shown that he had been greatly depressed, owingto his wife's illness, and a verdict of "Suicide during temporary insanity" was returned.

div.head: SERIOUS OMNIBUS ACCIDENT 'IN LONDON.
div.p: SERIOUS OMNIBUS ACCIDENT 'IN LONDON.

About half-past eight on Monday morning, an omnibus proceeding along Caledonian-road, Islington, was sud- denly overturned, when near King's Cross. It was fully loaded in and out, and several of the passengers were severely hurt. The sufferers were taken in a cab to the Royal Free Hospital, where two, Frank Jeffery, aged 50, and Walter Mabs) were detained suffering from disloca- tions. Some of the others were treated for cuts. The accident was caused by the breaking of the axle.

div.head: FUNERAL OF ROBERT BROWNING.
div.p: FUNERAL OF ROBERT BROWNING.

The remains of Robert Browning were laid to rest on Tuesday, in Westminister Abbey. They were removed at eleven o'clock from De Vere Gardens, followed by carriages containing members of the poet's family and those of his wife's. There were numerous and beautiful wreaths from distinguished friends and sympathiziers. including the Browning Societies of London and Bradford. The coffin bore the inscription : "Robert Browning, born May 7, 1812 • died Dec. 12, 1889." For a considerable time before the hour appointed for the interment the doors of the Abbcy were beset with crowds of ladies and gentlemen in mourning. The grave was dug in the Poet's Corner, near Cowley's monument, and just within the angle marked by the bust of Longfellow, and was surrounded by wreaths composed mostly of white exotics, with some of pink and purple. A procession of clergy and choristers met the body at the west cloister door, and the procession after- wards proceeded to the graveside, around which were disposed the Archbishop of Canterbury, Dean Bradley, Canon Prothero, Canon Duckworth, and other clergy, together with the pall bearers. The remainder of the choral service was then sung, and the committal to the grave and collect were said by the Dean of West- minister.

PRESENTATION T 6 A MA.NAGER AT
WARRINGTON.

Mr. William Reid, who retires from the manage- ment of the breweries of Messrs. P. Walker and son, after 29 years service with that firm, was on Mon- day evening presented, at the Woolpack Inn, War- rington, with a beautifully engraved silver salver and tea and coffee service. These handsome pre- sents had been subscribed for by the heads of the different departments of the brewery, and the managers of the vaults of Messrs.- P. Walker and Son. There was a large attendance at the pre- sentation. Mr. BAIRD, who made the presen- tation, said Mr. Reid's resignation had come rather suddenly upon them' but all the employes had willingly subscribed towards the mem- ento in recognition of Mr. Reid's past services.— Mr. REID said the presentation was a source of gratifica- tion to him. He had always done what he thought to be in the interests of the firm, and he had also done his best for everyone connected with the firm. (Applause.) Their Chairman was the oldest member at present con- nected with the firm, and he was sure that it was very gratifying to him (Mr. Reid), and would ke to his family, to receive such a handsome preset. He was sure it would be appreciated. He hoped things would go on as presperously as ever. The firm had been a success in the past, and he hoped it would be in the future. He again thanked them for their kindness. (Applause.)— Mr. A. POTTER apologised for the absence of several of the Liverpool representatives, who had sent word through the telephGne of their inability to be present. They would, he said, have taken great pleasure in com- ing to Warrington had they not been prevented. When the matter was first mooted, there was great hesitation as to how they should proceed. All wished to join in the memorial, and if they, had made it general; he did not know where it wotfld have finished. They had come to the conclusion that the best plan was to keep the memento strictly to the employes of Messrs. P. Walker and Son's breweries, and the old, members and managers of the firm, and of the vaults in Warrington and Liverpool. The goodwill which had been shown by every subscriber was very commendable. Mr. BROOKES said they all felt very keenly the retirement of their old manager, who was a particular friend of his, as ke had known him ever since he came to Warrington. They were having fresh people amongst them, but he dsubted if anyone could do better than Mr. Reid had done.—Mr. WELLS was pleased to endorse the cordial sentiments which had been expressed towards their late manager, Mr. Reid, who still had their best wishes and thoughts. (Applause.)—Mr. BAXTER also spoke, and the rest of the evening was spent in a convivial manner.

div.head: GLADSTON-E'S BIRTHDAY.
div.p: GLADSTON-E'S BIRTHDAY.

The eightieth anniversary of the birth of Mr. Glad- stone, was celebrated, on Sunday, at Hawarclen. The right hon. gentleman, who is in very good health, attended divine service in the parish church in the morn- ing, and read the lessons. The day being fine, there were a good many visitors, who, at the conclusion of the services, congratulated the hon. gentleman upon being so well. On Saturday and Sunday a very large number of telegrams and letters were received at Hawarden Castle. Among others was a congratulary message from the Prince and Princess of Wales, who telegraphed, "We offer you our sincere congratulations on the eightieth anniversary of your birthday." Messages were also sent by many of Mr. Gladstone's personal friends, including Lord Granville, Lord Rosebery, Lord Ripon, Mr. John Morley, Sir William Harcourt, &c. One telegram from Mr. Illingworth, M.P., was dated Alexan- dria, and read, "Warm congratulations from three Yorkshire members in Egypt." A large number of pre- sents have been received, including an illuminated address, signed by all the members except four, of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly. The members of the Liberal Reform Club, Liverpool, held a conversazione on Saturday afternoon, and a re- ception, to celebrate the anniversary of the birthday of Mr. Gladstone. Liberal Unionists and Gladstoman Liberals alike showed by their presence their personal regard for the right hon. gentleman. Visitors were re- ceived by Mr. and Mrs. Edward Evans, jun. Mr. Evans being chairman of the club, announced that the follow- ing congratulatory telegram had been sent to Mr. Glad- stone: The company assembled at the Reform Club, Liverpool, offer hearty congratulations to Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, on Mr. Gladstone attaining his eightieb.h year, and trust that Providence may spare his life fbr many years to come, to the advantage of his fellow-country- men." The Liberal party at Darwen, on Saturday night, celebrated Mr. Gladstone's birthday by a banquet, which was served in the Liberal Club, Market-st., D.rwen, when nearly 150 gentlemen sat down, the repast was a sumptuous one. CELEBRATION Al DERBY. Sir William Harcourt was, on Monday night, the principal speaker at a dinner attended by over 700 Liberals in Derby, in honour of the eightieth birthday of Mr. Gladstone. Sir William Harcourt in proposing Mr. Gladstone's health, said they were celebrating the eightieth birthday of a man whose name and fame would endure wherever and as long as the English tongue was spoken. The first quarter of Mr. Gladstone's life had been perhaps the most distressful known to the English nation, but the last period had been perhaps the most prosperous to the English nation, and of that prosperity he had been the principal author. The reason the Liberal party were prepared to follow Mr. Gladstone was• that, as the Irish people were with regard to O'Connell, they were really pursuaded that he was a man who had their interests at heart, and no effectual Government would make any progress until the people had made up their mind to trust a leader. Therefore, the Liber,..l party, believing in Mr. Gladstone, were prepared to follow him to the end. MESSAGE FROM THE KHEDIVE.

Throughout the whole of Monday the special staff S at the Hawarden Post Office were busily engaged in receiv- ing and delivering congratulatory telegrams and letters from all parts of the kingdom and from foreign coun- tries. The mass of correspondence has been unprece- dented this year, and it is no exaggeration to say that the right honourable gentleman has been thus felicitated by about 1,300 persons of all classes and creeds since Saturday last. Monday morning's post brought the fol- lowing letter from the Kedive : " Abdin Palace, Cairo, "17th December, 1889,

"Dear Mr. Gladstone,—l have the pleasure 'to offer you my sincere congratulations on the happy occasion of your birthday. I trust that many years may see this day come round and ever find you in the enjoyment of health and prosperity with your noble family. Allow me, dear Mr. Gladstone, to wish you a merry Christmas, with a happy and prosperous New Year.—l am, dear Mr. Gladstone, your friend,
"MEIIEMET TEWFIK,"
In the afternoon the Duke and Duchess of West- minster sent a congratulatory message with a bouquet of flowers. MR. GLADSTONE'S LETTER OF ACKNOWLEDG- MENT. .

even more imperative

'Sir,—! am under a necessity _ - than heretofore which obliges me to invoke your friendly aid in conveying my warm and grateful thanks to those who have honoured me on the occasion of my 80th birth- day with the expression of their congratulations, their good wishes, and their prayers on my behalf, or who have presented to me varied and valued memorials in token of their interest in the day. "It has not been possible,down to the present time, to count the arrivals, which are still in progress, but it is not less just than gratifying to say that they are not re- stricted by any limit of age, condition, country, or poli- tical party. lam also well aware how many there are on such occasions whose silence only means that they are reluctant to add to a mass the physical condition of which might, they think, be unmanageable. lam ever conscious that these congratulations are due to the itn- mense predominance of generosity and indulgence in the estimation of parliamentary and public labour, and to the large access, of sympathy due to the unexpected and unusual prolongation of•my period of service. " I will only add how sorry I am to offer so scanty and general an acknowledgment of so great a duty ; how I hope that these kindnesses may help to make me watch- ful in avoiding error ; and how heartily I return all the good words and sentiments which have been so largely showered upon Inc. " I have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, (Signed) W. E. GLADSTONE. " Hawarden, Dec. 30, 1889."

div.head: SECRET FOR YEARS.
div.p: A SECRET FOR YEARS.

CHAPTER XLIII. MRS'. FAIINCE WHISPERS A NA:qE. THE next morning Miss Ingestre's ab,ence was dis- covered. The servant had found her room empty, and her bed unoccupied. Her bonnet and cloak, too, were gone. Mr. Ingestre was from home, and Catherine at first seemed paralysed by the nev s. She ordered the lake to be dragged, the Woods searched. Anu die lake was dragged, and all the estate ridden over; but no Cleland was found.

Maxall laughed loudly at these proceedings, and laughed so significantly, that Catherine's suspicions instantly turned upon him as an agent in her dis- appearance. "You know where she is? You have hidden her somewhere?" "I do not know where she is; but I can guess pretty well," was the reply, accompanied by an insolent laugh. "Tell me directly—immediately, I beg." "Ask Ingestre to tell you, I shaa't ; " and lin turned his back on her. She wrote to the father word of what had happened, and his reply was brief: "Catherine I will search the world over to find and bring her back." She was compelled to remain satisfied with this; for nothing more could she do in the inadter. But the idea gained strength in her mind that Maxall was the instigator of the girl's fight, she believed it by many signs and tokens observed by her in the watch she kept upon him. Maxall knew that she watched him—knew her intent eyes followed his every movement He knew that she saw the faltering hand held forth of a morn- ing to take his coffee-cup from hers. He knew that she watched him while he drank as only men do Who have some horrible care to drown. He knew that she heard his step up and down that lonely room of his, where the cedar boughs grated on the window panes, and where a croaking raven waald perch on the pointed gable, in the dead of night, too, when all other birds slept—that room, where never a touch of undrugged sleep had blessed his burning eyeballs— where nightmare and phantom dreams were all he knew cif rest. Of all the heavy, sin-ridden hearts that house lied ever held, from the day when it first rose up a new and goodly pile, to the time when its rafters were black, and the moss of centuries filled the crevice's the tiled roof, never was heart in Redfern so sinful and so weary as that of the creole. Never, of all that Ingestre race, had a soul lain heavy beneath the stain of another's blood. And the groans and curses that fell from the murderer's lips in that room, where the first that stained and polluted the old oak panelling. Ile almost feared the boards in their very creaking would take the sound of a human voice and betray him. Three days went by; no letter from Mr. Ingestre, no news of Cleland. Catherine was alone at Redfern —a prey to wretched suspense and dreary inaction. She was sitting alone on the evening of the third day, awaiting Domingo's return from the village with the afternoon letters, when a servant entered the room to say some person desired very earnestly to speak with her. Befoie she could reply, almost before the man had delivered the message, he was thrust aside, arid ii tall female, dressed in black, entered. Catherine rose from her seat, and the woman curtsied respectfully. 'James seemed inclined to resent her abrupt entrance; but his mistress told him to leave the room and wait outside. "Servants are fond of listening, ma'am; better tell him to go quite away. / shall do you no harm, hie the man's tongue may, if he get gabbling about wile: I say to you." "I can trust the boy; he is no eavesdropper. now what is it you wish to say to me ? " The woman threw back her crape veil, and looked scrutinisingly at the speaker—looked at the graceful, bending figure—the pale, handsome face, ind. then at the small hand resting on the arm of the chair she had risen from. "Ali, you are not married to him yet, then?" she said, but not rudely. Catherine flushed deeply, and looked with something like haughtiness at the woman. " Wait ; don't be cross with me, madam, nor look as if You daren't be questioned. for I only wish to da you a kindness—a kindness you will thank me for when it's done." "And may I not know the name of the person to whom I shall stand indebted I" " Keziali Faunce is my name," was the answer. " What did you say?' "Kmiah Faunce, ma'am: Mr. Ingestre knows the name well." Then there was a pause. Catherine seemed at first astonished, and then incredulous. " Knish Faunce is well known to me by sight," she said. "I have seen her three times in my life, but she is certainly not like you." You have never seen see in your life before,
And

madam, and that I can swear. Fr the last five years I have not left the neighbourhood of London, and only came down to this place to day to warn you of the danger you are running into 'with your 'eyes shut." "Danger, my good woman! Tell me more plainly what your meaning is; I cannot bear enigmas. You know something of—" She stopped; her quiver- ing lips refused to utter the name. Tears were in her eyes, and her heart beat violently, for in the stern, inflexible face of the woman before her, she read some purpose as hard and inflexible as itself. "I have come a hundred miles from home to vdarn you not to marry George Ross Ingestre. Don't marry him, if you love your good name better than you do him! Don't marry him, if you would keep your heart unbroken and your soul fit for heaven! If you are a good and innocent woman, I say, don't marry him!" she cried, he.oming fast and fierce in her denunciation. "Don't marry him! He is an unprincipled man_a vile one! He has no good in his bad heart but the love of his children, and--" .But Catherine turned on her here. Be silent! How dare you abuse that 'man in hie own house, and in the presence of the woman fie has asked to he his wife! I will not listen to von; you are an impostor. Keziala Faunce is a fair woman, with yellow hair and a white face! I cannot comprehend the purpose of your visit here." Then you have seen a woman like that—yellow hair and a fair face—has a beautiful voice— you have seen her ? " "I have, and Mr. Ingestre told me her name." "Then he lied! When next you see him, tell him a tall, blamk-imired woman. vino said her name was Keziah Faunce, told you so; and tell him, too, that she did it to save him from a gaol. Arid as for you, madam, if you marry Mr. Inaeitre, you will (1,1 him the evilest thing that can beadone in this life. Th 3 Lori have mercy on•you both, then, I say, for man will have none." Catherine's blanched face turned slowly from the revealing light of the fire. She could not near that that strange woman should see her agony ; for tier tear of something nameless—s, horror =guessed at—was worse agony to bear than certainty. She said so, in a husky voice. "Speak plainer. Who and what are you, that yati should concern yourself about lam and me? "1 have told you my name before. lam weld og now but a sour-hearted woman; but onee upon a time, when I lived in this home as lady's-maid to the Mother of his children, I was soindhing different. And Why I trouble myself about this niiirriagi because I don't care'to think the harm that will r, tee of it might have been prevented by my speakiug a word in time." The woman was no impostor: the simple truth feline • simply enough from her lips. Catherine owned it, with a pang. ."rell me," she said, "one other thing; tell me the name of the woman I have called by yours." Mrs. Faunce shook her head. "I am afraid; the sound of it has not been heard for many a day." "Whisper it; I mast know." tt Come here, then, and I'll tell you." Catherine leant forward, and the woman whispered a name in her ear. tt Truth?'" "Truth." "Oh, mercy!" She sank on her knees, and remained there, with her hands clasped over her heart, and her wild ti 3. es fixed on the woman's face. "God help me!" she sighed, presently, but no more. Those few words sounded like the last and feeblest vibration of a broken chord—a chord that would new vibrate to music again. "God help you, indeed, and punish Mei But it will be punishment enough to have the woman he has set his wicked heaft on taken from him. I will go now, for I have done all the good it is in my power to do,,and I hope it will comfort me when I cone, to die." Here she walked towards the door, and timing round once, before she laid her hand upon the handle, said: "Forgive me- it I Dave sato otfensive.
ma not mean it, .tor 1 have no bact. teeing towaras
you, 11 or to him either. I only thought it my duty to tell you what you d:d not know." " Thank you you have saved me. Wait; you will stay and take food and rest." _
Her husky lips could scarcely form the words; but Kfitiah heard them.

"Eat and rest in this hou,e! No !" she cried fiercely. "not here; the food would poison me. Thank you oh the same. Good night, madam." . She went out into the dark night, across the dark park, and on to the same village, in the same path that Cleland had gone before her. And there was a third to follow yet. An hour after, Catherine took that same little beaten track through the wet grass, and de- scendA the village; but she walked on quickly, and soon left its lights far behind. CHAPTER X IV. CEOR T OR ROSS RIWITS A BATTLE, A) tOSTIg. MR. ItiOESTRE was alone in h's arart vents at the "Brunswick Hotel" when Catherine's 4ter was put into his hand, teltng him of his daughter's disap:war- anee. Masan told an untruth (not an une, airmen thing with him, as you may have acetic when he said the father probably knew of the whereaboul-s of his child. (ieorge Ingestre was on the eve of sittim4 down too late dinner; but he could taste nothing after such news from home. . . . ... .

Cle gone! Cle•run away l—the most affectionate girl that ever breathed, run away from a parent who loved her fondly—weakly! Be did not credit it. He believed that I\.laxall had quarrelled with her in an offensive manner, and that she had left the house in indignation to seek her father in London. She knew his address, and would no doubt be there before the night was out, lie would wait in that room for an hceir, and then start for the railway terrniaus and meet the next train from due S .
So he ate no dlnner, but walked up and elwn the room for an hour.

To have looked at that man's face, you would not have imagined him to be the happy bridegroom, that three shirt days would unite to the woman he loved —give to him her whom he craved above all other blessings on earth—to hiM whose life seemed a vain one reput from hers; eyesight dim, unless he saw' through her vish n ; thought coknirless, unless tinted with the reflex of her own. In three days! That was what he had been thinking about before the letter came. Three short days ! And he still thought of it, in spite of the strange news he had heard.

Hut his mind was scarcely uneasy about the girl; she was 140 sure to come to him—certain to make her way to him; she had threatpned it often when he left for London. So he waited the hour out, and thought of those three days—of what might come after them, of what had gone before them. He threw himself down in a chair at last, tired out, folded his arms, and looked at the clock on the mantel- shelf. _ _

I would that my pen could portray the face of that man, as he sat there looking at the clock, watching Time as it marched toward, past and away from him; watching it as he let it flee past, with the precious irrecoverable "now" in its grasp. It was the faco of one who disdains to look back, because remorse is unavailing, and who looks forward only to defy what Time is hurrying up- -the face of a strong man fighting with his mighty r assions—of a sinner wrestling with his sins, without avail. The clock struck, the hour of battle was gone, and the sinner's face was darkened with the conflict; the strong passions had overcome the strong man. It is well that we pray "Lead us not into temptation," for to the habitual sinner to be tempted is to tall; the battle is vain, the victory never won. Alas, for the lost!

He heard the clock strike, and knew that he must ge to the railway station. Be rose to get his hat, and put it on before the pier-glass; then he folded his arms and looked at himself—his great, handsome self, that God had moulded out of the strength and beauty of creation. In his might and manliness he stood, and thought how that beauty and might had served him in his half-done journey through the world. The smile was a bitter one as he turned away. "Yes, God made me comely, and I have made myself hideous. My passions are strongL r than my strong limbs, and have torn me worse than wolves could tear my flesh; they have been my enemies all through, and now—and now I am going to do what a madman might; but no sane man. How can I expect to escape? Catherine, I will kill myself at your feet, rather than a shadow of my guilt shall fall upon you. But it shall not; I have taken every pre- caution." He went out, got into a cab, and set off for the station. The train was due in ten minute. It came; he saw the passengers get out, from the first to the I last, but no Cleland:was among them. He turned away, went into a coffee-house close by, and wrote to Catherine the few words which we have _

given in the precedingschapter, Then hiflnrth - into the gas-lit street again, and cared little where his steps led him. He had felt so certain ihat his daughter would arrive by that train—so convinced that it was to his prmection she would tiy —saiesolute in the belief that her love for him would direct her to where he was, if, as he imagined, Bh3 was fro,luf under any trouble. But she had not come; and when ht ImAed again at Catherine's note, he found it was dated three dflys back. No, she had left him—flown from, and not to him; and he walked on in 11 bitter, reckless mood. Was he ?Ike that old hour, in the tilde, from which even the rats fled, prophesying its_fall ?

Men and women we're all I'7mnd hint, and the gas- lamps burning brightly overhead. Ile saw every- thing around him plain as day, and he shrank to thrh some man or woman should see the misery in his face., and jeer at it. The thought, or rather fear, maddened him, and as he elbowed his way through the crowd, in his frenzy, he lifted his hand and pushed a female out of his path, who was slow to let him hurry byl. She screamed and fell, and a waman whose arm she Seemed to hold staggered and fell tor,. They b•eth rose again quickly enough, and the tallest and aligl;test of the two clung to her companion. and would have hurried her on; but she tore herself from the yenne one's grasp; she flew back to the insulter, and ca!h-qt , him by all the horrible names her foul tongue coulkl utter. - Her yellow hair hung about her white face. her bonnet was tattered, her shawl unpinned, her speech was not clear, nor her person steady. The bystanders saw that the woman was not sober, so they laughed and passed on, for drunken women have a right to be pushed out of the way. For two minutes the foul torrent rushed out of her mouth; then her companion, who for those two minutes snemed to have been almost stunned, ran back, and attempted to drag her on. " Mamma ! mamma ! come away ! " And George Ingestre, the Squire of Redfern, rtW ; his only daughter clasp the drunken woman round the waist and drag her from the spot. Then the woman began to whimper, aud tottered away, hanging on ' Cleland's frail arm. And thus he came to know to whose shelter his i child had sown.

div.p: Mr. SIDNEYBALLIFAX, who also spoke in favour of the resolution, met with a very hearty reception. He said that although Mr. Gladstone had been in the public ser- vice for more than 56 years, he had throughout that • long period worn "the white flower of a blameless life." • kCheers.) His strength had been as the strength of ten, ' because his heart was pure; and, as Mr. Crosfield had ' reminded the meeting, "at the age of four score years his eye was not dimmed nor his natural force abated." Who was there whocould do justice to the grandeur of Mr. Gladstone's moral character? Who could do justice to his great genius forconstructivelegislation ? (Cheers.) And, as the Rev. John Yonge had said, thiswas an event which had been hailed with signs of appreciation alike by the Liberal and Tory press and by politicians °Lail shades of opinion. Only one voice was silent, and that wais the voice of the member for West Birmingham—Mr. Chamberlain, But if Mr. Chamberlain's was absent in the congratulations which were pouring in upon Mr. Glad- stone, there was, at least, one voice than which none was more sincere and hearty—the voice of the Irish people'. (Cheers.) It had been the speaker'sgood fortune to spend lengthened periods in Ireland for the purpose of examining into the working of Mr. Balf air's Coercion Act and into the land question. Wherever he went, no matter what part of the country, the first question put by, the peasants whose homes he visited was " How is he, sir?" A person did not need to ask " Who ? " There was only one " he " to the Irish peasant, and that was William Ewart Gladstone. (Cheers.) Not even Parnell or William O'Brien took precedence with them. (Hear, hear.) He did not remember having gone into a single hut where he had not found, even though it be from a cartoon in" United Ireland," some humble representa- tion of the noble face and features of the Grand Old Man. (Cheers.) The event they Were that evening celebrating was one of no ordinary political signific•ince, and the Liberals were in better spirits to-day than were the Tory party. The section of the party at that meeting was in better spirits than the meeting in the Public Hall the other night which the Attorney-General addressed. (Hear, hear.) The Tory party in Warrington must be, to use a vulgar term, very • 'down in the mouth" when thsy had to call in the ser- vices of her Majesty's Attorney General to cheer them up a bit and put a little fight into them. (Laughter and cheers.) He looked upon Sir Richard Webster as the political counterpart of one of the gravediggers in the play of "Hamlet." That Public Hall meeting reminded him of an incident which took place at a bye-election in the South of England a short time age. Before the election it was noticed that a sign in a local barber's shop read "Clean shave—one penny." After the con- test, the Liberal being where he ought to be, at the top of the poll, and the Tory at the bottom, the sign in the barber's window ran: "Clean shave—Liberals id., Conservatives, 3d." (Laughter and cheers.) The explanation vouchsafed was, that since the result of the election had become known, the Tories had had such long faces that there was more hair to takeoff. (Laugh- ter.) But though the meeting at the Public Hall was depressing to the spirits of Conservatives, the reports of the speeches were highly amusing to read. The Attorney-General said that the signs of renewed prosperity in this country were due to the fact that we had a Government which knew its own mind and stuck to it. The humour of such ani utterance became apparent when one remembered the conduct of the present Government with respect to the Van and Wheel Tax, Compensation to the Publicans, Sugar Bounties Bill, and the Tithe Bill. It would have been much mere satisfactory to the Radic9,ls of Warrington if Sir Richard Webster had had something to say in explan- ation of his action in withholding the consideration of the forged Parnell letters from the Special Commission weeks after it was known by the "Times "and their counsel that the letters had no foundation in fact. (Cheers.) He could not help noticing that Sir Richard had very little to say about the success of Mr. Balfour's policy in Ireland, because a complete change in regard to that matter had, within the last two or three weeks, come over the " Times " and other supporters of the Government. That cock-a-hoop cry of which we used to hear so • much had almost disappeared. What the Liberals had to complain of in the conduct of Irish affairs was that Mr. Balfour and the Government had been making war, not upon crime, but upon the undying spirit of Irish nationality—that nationality which, like a man's life, centred in the heart, and like the blood coursed through every vein and artery of the body. (Cheers.) And the Government could not be credited with having much sense if they thought that when better men had failed they were going to succeed in stamp- ing out that undying spirit of Irish nationality. (Cheers.) What was wanted and claimed was that the people of this country might have an opportunity, once and for all, to clear themselves from the guilt with which the present Government had stained the fair name of England during the past three years. The second part of the resolution that he was supporting said the meeting " fervently hopes that Mr. Gladstone will for many years to come continue to display untiring energy and zeal in carrying out tiose measures of reform which are so urgently desired, and especially a measure of Home Rule for Ireland." Mr. Gladstone's seal was affixed to mea- sures of reform ; the Liberal party, therefore,could go for- ward to them with a good heart. But befor they could be attempted there was something else to be done. The legislative axe must be sharpened, and the legisla- tive machinery must be put in good condition. An important crisis had been reached in our history, not alone in relation to Ireland, but to the people of this country. During the long course of ages the laying of the foundation stones of this mighty empire, and the building up of our constitution,had gone slowly on. We could safely challenge any country to produce a more glorious history. There had, it was true, been moments when the sun of liberty had been well-nigh totally eclipsed but, ever and anon, the stillness of the night had been broken by the voice of one and another raised up to set the people freo. (Cheers.) But there had all the while been two black spots upon the name and fame of our country. One had been the standing reproach that we had by us a country in the condition of Ireland,. and the other had been that at our very doors there had existed such deep and widespread poverty, aide ,by side with the signs of advancing' wealth. The Liberal party demanded for the one, in the words of Grattan, "continued severance of the two Parlia- ments in order to ensure the continued and ever- lasting unity of the empire." (Cheers.) They were enabled to assure their fellow-country men in Ire- *lnd that after seven long centuries of bfoodshed,famine, and strife, after the long night of national iniquity, the grey streak of dawn had come; at last for them had the dawn lifted and the shadows fled away. (Cheers.) Their English friends, the Liberal party, bade them be of good courage, for their emancipation was at hand ; and when that was effected, they would claim, as they claimed now, that the alliance of the two democracies having become indissoluble, their interests were hence- forward one and indivisible—(cheers)—and they de- manded what they were already assured of, the help of the Irish in bettering the condition of the English people. (Hear, hear.) The. Liberals sought for all, not the luxuries of the few, but all the necessaries, and some of the comforts of life at present denied to many. They desired that the people should have better homes,.anil purer dwellings, in order that they might be better men. They sought, also, to shorten excessive hours of toil. They had no wish to embark upon a spirited foreign policy, their desire being to improve the condition of the people at home. (Cheers.) The resolution was then put to the meeting, and car- ried unanimously. ' Councillor Wm. PIERPOINT proposed, and Councillor r FLOOD seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. liallifax, Mr. Crosfield, and the Rev. John Yonge for their speeches. The proposition was passed with cheers..

The "ley. Jonx YOI:IGE and Mr. HALIFAX replied, and the latter moved that a similar compliment be paid the Chairman for his services. This motiorovras seconded by Councillor FLEMING, and carried by acclamation, after which the meeting con- cluded.

div.head: IS DR. PETERS ALIVE?
div.p: IS DR. PETERS ALIVE?

BERLIN, . TUESDAY NIGHT—The following telegram from Zanzibar, dated yesterday, appears in the Ber- liner Tageblatt." "The Peters expedition has not been massacred, but is, according to statements just arrived at Zanzibar, on the march bet Ween Mount Kenia and Lake Baringo. In Vituland everything is quiet." kyLake Baringo is fifty geographical miles W.N.W of Mount Kenia. The above telegram does not say who received the message, or from it originates, so that one cannot judge whether it is trustworthy.

div.head: NEW YEAR'S HONOURS.
div.p: NEW YEAR'S HONOURS.

Dixon, late Mayo? of Middlesbrough; Mr. Robert P. Harding, Chief Official Receiver in Bankruptcy ; Mr. Thomas Sowler, Man- chester, and gentlemen 'holding Indian and Colonial appointments. Promotions are also made in the several orders of distinction.

div.head: EXA MINER, SATURDA.Y, JANUARY 4, 1890.
div.p: THE EXA MINER, SATURDA.Y, JANUARY 4, 1890.
DEATH OF THE EX-EMPRESS OF BRAZIL. _

The ex-Empress of Brazil died at Oporto on Saturday' afternoon. She had been suffering from a variety ot disorders for some time. Her Majesty, who was daugh- ter of Francis 1., late King of Naples, was married to Dom Pedro on September 4, 1843.
FOUR ENGLISHMEN EATEN BY CANNIBALS.

Mail advices from an Francisco received at Queens- town state that intelligence had reached there on Dec. 23rd that the mate and three seamen of the British schooner Enterprise where killed and eaten by cannibals, at Hammond Island, one of the Solomon Group, on October 29th, and that news of the massacre having been carried to Captain Hunt, of Her Majesty's corvette Royalist, he shelled the villages on the island.
THREE EXECUTIONS IN ONE DIY.

The dbuble execution of Robert West, 45, travelling showman, and Frederick Brett, 39, labourer, who were recently sentenced to death for thewilful murder a their wives, at Sheffield and Halifax respectively, took place on Tuesday morning, at ebs-ht -o'clock, in the Armley Prison, near Leeds. Both men since receiving their sentence have appeared perfectly resigned to their fate, but have not made any confession or spoken about the crimes in any way. The prison chaplain has attended to West, while Brett, who was a Roman Catholic, had many in- terviews with the Rev. Father. Malcahy, and both men have devoted much of their time to devotional exercises. A few minutes before eight o'clock, the executioner, Billington, of Bolton, pinioned the men, and the solemn procession, headed by the under-sheriff and the governor of the gaol, and flanked by a number of warders, soon reached the scaffold. The men were placed side by side on one trap, and on the bolt being drawn the two fell simultaneously. Death in both cases appeared to be instantaneous. William Thomas Hook, 40, was executed within Maid- stone Gaol on fuesday morning for the murder of his wife Julia, at Gravesend, on September 18, 1889. Berry was the executioner. Since his condemnation the prisoner had listened to the ministrations of the prison chaplain, but had been callous, and expressed no repentance for his crime. During the past week he had been visited by a man named Jack Scott and his two young children, who are now inmates of the Coxheath Union. Between them and the prisoner a heartrending scene took place. The Sheriff, Mr. Joseph Sebag Montefiore, arrived ivl Maidstone on Monday night, and proceeded to the goa at seven o'clock in the morning. The prisoner rose early, and was immediately seen by the chaplain. He ate a fair breakfast and, when the executioner visited him, submitted to the pinioning with tranquility. The gal- lows is situated about 50 yards from the condemned cell, and the prisoner walked firmly to it. Berry then adjusted the white cap, and the prisoner, with great emotion, then said," Goodbye, Jack Scott; good bye, all my old friends. Now for the great secret. Julia, I loved you, my darling. Good bye, good bye, Julia; God bless you." The prisoner weighed about 12 stone, and a drop of eft. 2in. was allowed. Death was instan- taneous."

div.head: TWO MEN POISONED IN WALES.
div.p: TWO MEN POISONED IN WALES.

A sad case of poisoning is reported from Wales On New Year's Eve a young man visited Mr. Hussey, head bailiff at Old Park Farm. near Swansea. Hussey sent for a jar of beer, but the servant brought a jar contain- ing sheep dip. The visitor on taking a drink said it had a queer taste. Hussey thereupon took a draught, and, discovering the mistake, sent for the doctor. Remedies were of no avail, and the unfortunate men died on Wednesday. •

div.head: ARRESTED FOR MURDER.
div.p: ARRESTED FOR MURDER.

The county authorities at Airdrie on Wednesday received information of a supposed murder in the vil- lage of Eastfield. Captain Stewart and Inspector Mackay drove to the scene, and caused the arrest of two brothers named Quigley. Patrick Quigley, a miner, returning homelate on New Year's Eve, quarrelled with his mother and the younger brother and a sister joined in the dis- pute. When the neighbours came in Patrick was kick- ing his mother on the head, and she was picked up dead.
THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.

The influenza epidemic, while remaining stationary in Paris, is reported to be spreading in the outskirts of the city, and to prevail n the departments, but is not of a serious character. Owing to the spread of the malady in Lower Austria, the schools are to remain closed until the 7th inst. In Cassel the disease is generally extending, and doctors and chemists are reported to be busier than they have ever been before.

LONDON. The diplomatic corps generally has been attacked by influenza. The first to be taken was Count Hatzfeldt, German ambassador, who has been laid up for nearly a fortnight, Lord Salisbury is now bufferina at Hatfield, and Sir Philip Currie, private secretary at the Foreign Office. The Hon. Francis Villiers is also laid up. The complaint has also spread to less prominent officials.
THE LITE MR. EDWARD BOLTON. THE FUNERAL.

--- The remains of the late Mr. Edward Bolton' of Whitecross House, Bank Quay, were interred in the Friends Burying ground, Penketh, on Monday after- noon, in the presence of a number of friends, employes and others, iincluding the Revs. S. Wilkinson. E. S. Jackson, J. G. Richards, T. E. Winder; Messrs. Robert Garnett, William Darby- shire C. Jackson Holmes, Mr. Glendinning, Mr. and Mrs. W. D. Jeans, Mr. H. J. Longton (solicitor to the deceased), Mr. H. Brown, Mrs. Gumersall, Miss Ellen Robinson, of Liverpool. The funeral procession left White Cress House at about two o'clock, in the following order :—First carriage, containing Mrs. G. Y. Bolton, Miss Bolton (daughter of the deceased), Miss H. Bolton (niece), Miss Yates; second carriage, Lieut- Colonel G. Y. Bolton (son), Dm A. Bolton, J.P., of Johannesberg (son), Mr. W. Bolton, Captain Hogarth ; third carriage, Mr. H. Bolton (son), Mr. F. Bolton (son), Dr. Spinks ; fourth carriage, Mr. and Mrs. G. H. Bolton, Penketh ; Rev. S. Wilkinson, Mr. James Bolton; fifth carriage, Mrs. Wylde, Mr. C. E. Barlow. At the graveside Miss Ellen Robinson offered up prayer, and in the meeting-house a portion of Scripture was read by Mr. C. J. Holmes and an address delivered by Miss Robinson, after which the funeral ceremony was brought to a conclusion. The coffin, which was supplied by Messrs. Garnett and Co., was of fumed oak, with brass mountings, and bore the insaip- tion :—" Edward Bolton, born January 19, 1823; died December 26, 1889." The funeral arrangements were carried out by Messrs. Holmes and Powell, of Bridge-st., Warrington. Wreaths had been forwarded by Mrs. Bolton (widow), Mr. and Mrs. G. H. Bolton, Mr. and Mrs. J. Wylde, Mr. and Mrs. G. Y. Bolton, Mrs. Wilkin- son, Mrs. Matthew Wells (Sale), Dr. and Mrs. pinks;S the sons of the deceased, Miss Bolton, Colonel and Mrs. Wilson, Mr. and Mrs. Beaton, Miss C. Yates, Miss C. E. Bolton; and "as a memento of respect from the glass cutters and engravers" a wreath made of china, stand- ing on an imitation marble pedestal, surmounted by an oval glass.

div.head: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS.,
div.p: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS.,

MR. PARNELL THE CO-RESPONDENT. A petition for divorce has been filed by Captain William O'Shea, of 124, Victoria-street, Westminster, and justice of the peace in county Clare, against his wife; Mr. Charles Stewart Parnell, M.P., being co-respondent. The grounds alleged are the adultery of Mrs. O'Shea,dur- ing the period from April, 1888, up to the date of the petition, at the undermentioned places—Eltham, 34, York-terrace, Regent Park; Brighton, and Aldiugtou, Essex. No damages are claimed. It is stated that the petition was filed by Captain O'Shea on the 24th inst. A Dublin correspondent telegraphs—The annouire- ment of Captain O'Shea's divorce suit against his wife, with Mr. Parnell as co-respondent, has caused quite a sensation in Dublin. The relations of Mr. Parnell with Mrs. O'Shea, however, have been matter for conjecture and gossip for years past, though on in-re than one occa- sion Captain O'Shea has contradicted rumours which were current on the subject. The friendly relations be- tween the two gentlemen were broken off some time ago. Mrs. O'Shea is a daughter of the second Sir Matthew Wood, and a sister of Sir Evelyn Wood, the distinguished soldier. She was married to Captain O'Shea (formerly of the 18th Hussars), in 1887, and has borne him five children. INTERVIEW WITH CAPTAIN O'SHEA. A representative 'of the "Evening News and Post," called upon Captain O'Shea at his rooms, 124, Victoria- street, Westminster, on Saturday morning, and the captain at once frankly stated that the above news was true. The representative was shown up into a cosy aitting-room. Breakfast was on the table, and Captain 0 Shea's son was present. "We have received a report from a well-informed source," said the representative, "that you have insti- tuted an action for divorce, but owing to the gravity 1) f the announcement, my editor thought it but courteous to yourself not to publish it without corroboration from your own mouth." Uaptain O'Shea looked straight into the representa- tive's face and said, "I may as well say it is true.' " And that Mr. •Charles Stewart Parnell is the co- respondent ?"—" That is true too. But hew the deuce did you hear of it P"—Our representative did not ex- plain. " And is it also true," he pressed on, "that you do not claim damages ?" "Of course Ide not," said Captain O'Shea. He added, "I am much obliged to your editor for having the courtesy to ask me before publishing the fact." A DENIAL FROM MR. HOUSTON. Mr. Parnell having stated to a press representative that he hail received information that Captain O'Shea had been incited to bring his action for divorce by Mr. Houston, and that it was due to political motives, Mr. 'Houston, wnting on Monday afternoon, deniesthe state- ment that he has incited Captain O'Shea to institute divorce proceedings against Mr. Parnell, and states that I he was in total ign)rance of the proceedings until Satur- day morning, when all the world Icnew it:

div.head: CITATION SERVED,
div.p: THE CITATION SERVED,

The Press Association- states that Mr. Parnell was at hree o'clock on Thursday afternoon served with the itation and copy of petition in the suit for divorce brought by Captain O'Shea against his wife and against Mr. Parnell as co-respondent. Service was effeeed by Mr. Day. solicitor to Captain O'Shea, who attended per- sonally at the offices of Messrs. Lewis and Lewis, Ely- place, Holborn, at the above-named hour, in response to a communication from Messrs. Lewis. There was no one else present with the exception of two of Messrs. Leviis's clerks. Mr. Parnell, on receiving the docu- ments, made no observation.

Mr. Parnell will, it is stated, attend a meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party to be held shortly before the meeting of Parliament, and deny to the full the allega- tions involved in Captain o,'Shea's petition.

div.head: BANK QUAY WORKINGMEN'S MISSION
div.p: BANK QUAY WORKINGMEN'S MISSION
CHAPEL.

The annual public teapeeting in connection with this chapel took place in the schoolroom on Monday evening. At the tea there were about 140 persons present, the tables being presided over by Mesdames J. Hough, T. Dale, D. Monks, J. Monks, T. Ashley, D. Hill. S. Hill, Williams, Pawson, J. Hassell, and Miss L. Ashley. After tea a well-attended gathering was held, at which the chair was taken, in the early part, by Alderman Crosfield, and later on by Alder- man Davies. Mrs. Crosfield was also present. The meeting having been duly opened. Mr. T. ASHLEY, the secretary, read the annual report in which he said they were pleased to compare favour- ably with previous years. Everything was going on well. They had there a society class, with about 40 member; and they had also a mission band which they believed was doing a good work in going out in the open air distributing tracts and speaking to the people and inviting them to the chapel. They were pleased to say that all their seats were tree and unappropriated. Books were also provided. Recently their benches had been filled to their utmost limit, so much so that they had been compelled to place the young people around the communion rail. ' With regard to their financial affairs, last year they had a balance of £1 3s. 11id. in hand, and with their collection once a month and anniversary collections, they had an income of £29 55., while their expenses for carrying on the work this year had been £29 lid., leaving a small balance of 4s. 10s. This expenditure had been made up of preachers railway expenses, hymn and music books, cleaning, &c. As their chapel was truly named the Workingmen's Mission that money came from the workingmen of that thickly populated district of Bank Quay, which, he thought he would not be wrong in saying, had, since the Chairman erected the chapel in 1871, doubled its population. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said he was sorry to say that he had very little time to stay as he had to go to Wycliffe Hall to propose the first reso- lution there. He dare say his friend on the right (Alder- man Davies) would not approve of it—(laughter)—but he had to propose the health of William Ewart Gladstone —(applause)—to congratulate him on having attained his 80th birthday on the previous day: He should there- fore have to ask them to excuse him In a few minutes, but while he was away his place would be a great deal better occupied than he could fill it by the worthy alder- man himself. (Applause.) They knew that Ise and Alderman Davies had travelled a great deal together— 'he daresay they had been half way round the world together, and the passengers on board the steamerlsome- times got a little mixed. They could not tell which of the two aldermen was the other—(laughter)—because Alderman Davies called him the alderman, and he called Alderman Davies the alderman. He always called his friend alderman, because he looked upon him as pre- eminently " the" alderman. (Hear, hear.) He did not I put any alderman before him. Leaving alone the alder- men in Warrington and in Lancashire, he did not even I put any alderman in London before his friend Alderman Davies. (Applause.) He was pleased to meet them as usual at this season of the year. He was sure it must be a great comfort and pleasure to them when they attended the chapel close by, and when they came sometimes, as he had no doubt they did, to see their children so well taken care of on a Sunday. He had often told them that they were very much indebted to the teachers who devoted themselves so willingly to the instruc- tion of their children. He was glad to hear from the treasurer's report that the finances were in a flourishing state, and that there was a balance of 4s. 10d. to the good. So long as their expenses were below their in- chme they were pretty sure to go on all right, and it was very much to their credit that they were able amongst themselves to raise sufficient income to maintain their services and to keep their chapel clean and in good order. Ile".-oped that the coming year would be a pros- perous one for them, and that they should see more and more good done in that neighbourhood by means of that workingmen's chapel and that school. He was glad to find that there was an effort being made to teach the young women in connection with the Sunday School to sew. A sewing class was being established, and they were going to enlarge the vestry rooms at the back, so that they might bave better accommodation. He was sure it would be a very valuable thing to many a girl if she could be taught to sew. It was very necessary in- deed in these days for girls to learn both to sew and to cook, and he hoped that beforek long, at the People's College, there would be a cooking class established. They were making efforts now to get the money, and it would prove of great value to the town, because, after all, the comfort of a workingman's house depended principally upon the kind of wife he had got. If she was clever with her needle, could cook well, and knew how to make the money go without waste, it added a great deal to the working-man's comfolit, and there was no doubt what- ever in his wind that many a 'working-man was driven out of his home because of the absence of comfort there. Therefore, he believed that the teaching of the girls , in the manner they intended to teach them would prove to the cornier generation a great blessing. (Loud applause). Alderman DAVIES, on taking the chair, addressed a few remarks to those present. Alluding to the address of Alderman Crosfield, he said that it was his opinion that if a young woman would learn to cook well and to sew well she would map a good husband. (Laughter.) He had been interested in the report and he noticed that they did very well with their money for they had spent it almost to the ' last farthing. He would, however, add a sovereign to their balance of 4s. 10d. (Applause.) The year 1889 that was just passing away was a very extra- ordinary 'year, for the reason that it was the first of a series of 111 years in which the figure nine would have to be used in expressing them. Referring to their travels together, Alderman Davies said that Alderman Crosfield was always very particular in stating things exactly as he saw them, and if they were to look at his note-book they would find the facts recorded without any exaggera- tion, but they would find his (Alderman Davies') exactly the opposite, because he did not give so very much for a traveller unless •he could see what did not take place. (Laughter.) The musital'part of the programme was very success- fully rendered. It was opened with a chorus by the choir, and afterwards Mr. Mills sang "'The Stowaway " in good style. Later on Mr. IVliils gave a sysnpathetic rendering of the fine song" Love's Golden Dream." Miss L. Ashley sang "Another Day," and "Be true to me," and for these efforts she was warmly applauded. Two songs were given by Mr. Fanshaw, in both of which he was very successful, and for the first of which the audience would fain have had an encore. 'The recitations of Mr. Bevan were much-admired performances and deserved the commendations passed upon them by the Chairman. The first was "The losp of the S.S. London," and the second "Selections froth the Lady ot Lyons." "Our Evening Prayer" was nicely sung by Miss TilliOg, and a recitation "rho factory chimney," was meritoriously sebnaitted by Miss E. Tilling. Mr. F. Williams gave a humorous topical song, one of the allusions of which was to the unmade condition a many of the streets at Bank Quay. At the conclusion, Alderman CROSFIELD moved a vote of thanks to Alderman Davies for presiding, and this having been seconded by Mr. DALE was heartily accor- ded and duly acknowledged.
