div.head: TERRIBLE CALAMITY AT A POOR-LAW SCHOOL N EAR LONDON. 26 BOYS SUFFOCATED.
div.p: TERRIBLE CALAMITY AT A POOR-LAW SCHOOL N EAR LONDON. 26 BOYS SUFFOCATED.

Whilst the bells from,a score of London churches were proclaiming to the inhabitants of Forest-gate the advent of the New Year, a series of heartrend- ing scenes were being enacted close at hand. Shortly after half-past twelve o'clock, just as merry peals which followed various watchnight services were dying away, the notes of a solitary bell, obvi- ously rung by an unskilled hand, fell upon the ears of such belated wayfarers as happened to be in the vicinity of Forest-gate Poor-law SchooL The un- wonted sound did not continue long, for all hands were needed to assist in the work of rescue; but public attention was soon attracted to the spot by more powerful evidence of disaster, and the news rapidly spread that tire had broken out in the schools, and that lives were in danger. No time was lost by the local fire brigade in grappling with the situation. But the flames had secured a firm hold of the interior of the woodwork before the outbreak was discovered, and all that remained for the firemen to do was to try and limit the area of the conflagra- tion as much as possible and to render what help they could in getting the inmates out alive. Un- fortunately, a considerable number of lads had already perished. At great personal risk, the attend- ants, who had been awakened by ringing of the bell and the piteous appeals for help, had struggled bravely against the stifling fumes which threatened the occupants of the burning rooms, and had brought a large proportion of the boys out of danger; but nearly 30 remained unaccounted for, and 25 of these were dead before the rescue party could get them to the open air. One little boy suc- cumbed as he was being carried out. The range of buildings is situated in extensive grounds facing the Great Eastern Railway, about half way between Ferest Gate, and Maryland Point stations, on that systern. The institution, which is intended for the reception of pauper and refractory children from unions in the east end of London, accommodates about 600. and at the time of the outbreak nearly all the beds were occupied. It was in the wing of the main building, known as the dining room annexe, that the fire origin- ated. The wing is an erection of three floors, and, in view of an occurrence such as that which took place on Wednesday morning, it is furnished with an external stone staircase in addition to the usual mode of access from the main building proper. The fire originated in the needle room on the ground floor, and it is supposed to have bmn caused by the overheating of the flue attached to the stove. About half-past twelve Miss Julia Bloomfield, who had retired to rest some time before, became aware of the presence of smoke in her bedroom. On reaching the door of the needle room, of which she always carries a key, she saw a light shining through a crevice near the floor, and a moment later, having opened the door, she saw that the plank partition was on fire. To fetch the dinner bell and ring it outside one of the windows was the work of a very few seconds. Miss Bloomfield then ran upstairs to the bedroom of Miss Terry, the needlework mistress, who fetched the dining-room keys from the official in whose charge they remain at night. The two women having given an alarm to the other servants sleeping in the wing, hurried downstairs again to rouse the super- intendent, Mr. Duncan. Unlocking the dining-room door, they made their way into the main building, whence access to most distant rooms was easy. Miss Terry fetched Mr. Duncan and the schoolmistress, and Miss Bloomfield gave the alarm to other officials. In consequence of the careful precautions taken to prevent communication between the boys' dormitories and the servants' rooms adjoining, it was impossible for Miss Bloomfield to warn the sleeping children, and, until. Mr. Duncan arrived on the scene and

unlocked the door, things were at a standstill. He saw at once that the fire had obtained too sure a footing for any efforts of his to avail in extinguishing it, and appreciating the terrible peril which threatened those overhead, he made a dash for the staircase and succeeded, despite the smoke, in reaching the first floor dormitory where 30 boys, of ages varying from seven to ten lay asleep. He unlocked the door and took a couple of steps forward, with the intew ion of entering the room, but it was too late. By this time the flooriug was on fire, and the draught caused a rush of smoke to the open door, with the consequence that Mr. Duncan was literally torced beckon to the staircase. Although half suffocated by the noxious fumes, he essayed a second time to reach his charges, but again in vain. This time he was completelyoverpowered, and losing consciousness, he fell to the ground. In the purer air near the floor he quickly revived, and other officials who had now come up joined him in endeavouring to battle with the fumes, but their hydrants and portable extinguishers had little effect in staying the progress of the outbreak. An attempt to force an entrance at this point had eventually to be abandoned until the fire bad been practically got under. Meanwhile operations were being carried on at the other end of the wing with much better success. George Hare, the yardman, who sleeps in the upper dormitory on the second floor, went to bed about half-past nine. After sleeping about three hours he awoke, to find his room full of smoke, and to hear some of the little fellows in the adjoining apartment calling to him. He jumped out .of bed and went into the dormitory, where he found a few of the boys awake and up; but a considerable proportion of the remainder were asleep, and unconscious of any danger. The end of the room nearest to the doorway was thick with smoke, and the door had to be closed without delay for fear of worse consequences. The lads bythis time becoming helpless through frightand suffoca- tion, and Hare had almost to use force to get them to the top of the other staircase. Taking one of the youngest boy; on each arm, and calling to the others to follow, he made his way down the wooden stairs to the first floor, where the state of things appeared to be even worse. The door at the bottom of the external staircase had, however, by this time been forced from the outside, and help was at hand. Having deposited his first burden in safety, he groped his way back to the upper floor and got' a number of boys down by making them join hands and follow hiin. The fire never obtained so fierce a hold on the second floor dormitory as on the one below, yet of the 54 boys who slept at the top of the building only 40 were brought out alive. There was probably net a single case of painful death in this dormitory. In the lower room two of the children appeared to have expired in great agony, their limbs being drawn and their fea- tures distorted. Here, also, the bodies were in some in- sauces found on the floor or even under the beds. Above, however, all those who were awakened to the sense of their peril appeared to have escaped, the condi- tion of those who perished being in itself proof that death came upon them whilst asleep. The fatality in the lower dormitory was much heavier than in the' upper one, only 14 of the 30 lads quartered there being got out alive. When an entrance was once effected, the firemen and others made superhuman efforts, and some very narrow escapes are on record; but pluck was of no avail when the rescuers were so handicapped in point of time. There is little doubt that the bulk of the deaths took place before the outbreak was discovered either by Miss Bloomfield or Mr. Hare, and, under these circumstances, unstinted praise should be given to those who so willingly risked their lives on behalf of the poor little waifs. When the steam engines arrived on the scene, a mastery was rapidly obtained over the fire, but it was not until after two o'clock that it was completely extinguished. The whole of the bodies, however, had been got out some time before this, and the authorities' were able to realise the full extent of the calamity. As the bodies were removed from the burning wing, they were taken to the infirmary, one of the smaller blocks of buildings. In accordance with time honoured custom, Wednesday was to have been a day of festivity for the scholars. A gigantic Christmas tree had been prepared for the amusement of the youngsters, and the crowd at the gates was swelled by many friends of the inmates who had come to witness the presentation of the prizes and other functions which form part of the New Year's Day programme. Of caurse the dreadful calamity which had befallen the schools upset the whole of the arrange- ments.

div.head: OPENING OF THE INQUEST.
div.p: OPENING OF THE INQUEST.

The coroner's inquiry into the circumstances attendiag the deaths of the 26 boys who were suffocated early on New Year's morning, at West Ham Industrial School, Stratford, was opened on Thursday. The coroner,Mr. C. L. Lewis, said it was understood that the evidence given that day would be merely as to the identification of the bodies. A large number of the public crowded at the entrance to the school gardens, and endeavoured unsuccessfully to gain access to the building. The in- quiry was held in the girls' schoolroom. Several members of the board of governors were present, including the chairman, Mr. H. J. Cook. Mr. H. E. Davies (fire expert and surveyor to the coroners of Middlesex and the city of London) also attended. Those relatives of the deceased who attended were conducted to seats by the deputy chaplain (Mr. Cowen), and several appeared overcome with griet. Inspector Isaac Thompson repre- ' sented the police. Mr. Charles Duncan, superintendent of the school, was the first witness examined. He said the whale of the children retired to bed at a quarter to eight on Tues- day night, that being the accustomed time. Nothing unusual happened until he was called at 35 minutes past twelve. On being roused from bed he was told by Miss Terry, the needle mistress, that. the needle room was on fire. He at once passed down the stairs and took the fire extinguisher with him. He tied a pockethandkerchief over his nose and mouth, groped on his knees, and threw the chemicals on the fire, which he saw at the top left-hand corner of the wooden partition dividing the needle room and the wardrobe room. The smouldering wood broke into a flame while he was there. It was neara stove pipe. The fire sub- sided a little after he had played on it—first with an

extinguisher, and then with a hvdrant.—The Coroner asked where Mr. Duncan first found the boys Had been suffocated. Witness said it was after 'MI had played on the fire that he learnt some Aft the boys were still in the two dormitories. "Vieperson having a key was sleeping that night within No, a, as the official by whom such keys were usually held happened to be on leave ; the boys, therefore, were locked in from that end, but did not know whether the exit was free by the other staircase. It was half-past one o'cleck when a number of bodies were recovered and taken to the infirmary. Ile was now able to identify seven bodies. Questioned by theforeman,witness said it was owing to the smoke that he did not at first discover fire in the partition.--By Mr. Nairn: Around the stone pipe was an iron collar separating it from the wood- work, and between the collar and pipe was four inches space. On this night there was an officer in No.lo, who had keys, and who, on ordinary eccasions could come downstairs and open No. 9, letting out boys by the ex- ternal staircase. .

Edward O'Brien, drill master, was next examined, and. identified six bodies.—Therza Pownall, nurse, identified the remaining 13, making with those identified by the superintendent, in all 26. The Coroner saitl that was the length to which he proposed to carry the inquiry that day. It was for the Jury to say when they would reassemble.—On the suggestion of the foreman, the inquiry was adjourned until Wednesday. .•. .
The interments will take place on Monday, at West Ham Cemetery.

div.head: POLEGATE TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE POLEGATE TRAGEDY.

The inquest was resumed at Polegate, near Eastbourne, on Thursday, on the two girls named Taylor, who were murdered by their mother. Evidence was given by several little children as to having fetched drink for the prisoner on the day of the crime. It was also stated that, although she had some property, she owed people mmey. A verdict of wilful murder was returned.— Kate Taylor, sister of the muredered girls, died onThurs- day night at the Princess Alice Memorial Hospital, Eastbourne, from injuries caused by her mother on the night of the murder. The third victim of the tragedy had had a silver tube inserted in her lacerated throat, and it was hoped she would recover. Mrs. Taylor will new be charged with triple murder.
BOATING ACCIDENT IN THE MENAI STRAITS.-FOITR LIVES LOST.

Mr. R. Jones Roberts, the coroner for Anglesey, on Tuesday, held an inquest at Beaumaris, relative to The death of John Hughes, a farm steward, who with three other persons was drowned by the capsizing of a boat in Menai Straits. The boat started from Beaumaris about eight o'clock on Sunday night, all her occupants being more or less under the influence of drink. About noon, on Monday the boat, half tilled with water, and without oars, was found on the shore about two miles from Beaumaris. The body of the deceased was found on Tuesday morning, near the weir at Lleiniog. It was surmised thst the men lost control over the boat, which drifted against a causeway of stones, and capsized. A verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was returned. By the accident 19 orphans and two widows are left,Httehes being the father of nine children, and John Williams, a keeper, leaving ten. The other two mm who were drowned were brothers named Williams, who lived at Tygwyn, Penmon.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS AND THE – NEW BILL. THE RATEPAYERS IN THE DARE.
div.p: THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS AND THE - NEW BILL. THE RATEPAYERS IN THE DARE.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, held gn Tuesday, the CLERK (Mr. J. C. Sutton, C.C.), referred to the Bill that is being promoted in Parliament by the War- rington Corporation. He had, he said, tried to follow that Bill, but be was sorry to say of their Town Council that he did not find by the newspaper reports—which were no doubt given fully and satisfactorily as far as the newspapers were con- cerned—that amount of information upon import- ant questions that came before the Council which he remembered used to be given a quarter of a century back. It seemed to him that the pouncil took to themselves, it might be properly, A some- what exclusive method of dealing with these ques- tions. At least, whatever might be done in com- mittee, there was not imparted to the ratepayers, who were materially concerned, that degree of information that would be useful, and, it seemed to him, would be proper to give. Any way it was not so complete as it used to be. Having followed as well as he could the observations that had been pub- lished as the proceedings ot the Town Council, lie found that the Bill was one of very great import- ance. div.head: QUESTION OF BOUNDARY.
div.p: THE QUESTION OF BOUNDARY.

His own view of the Bill was this: he did not know whether it would ultimately be an advantage to the town for the borough to be extended to the Slap Canal. In these days of trading and manufacturing competitien,it was an important question to people who wanted to establish business places and manufactories, to know the rates of the district and liabilities as to debt, the cost of necessaries sueli as gas, and it was a question whether it would be encouraging to sub- stitute for the present rural rating and rural exer- cise of authority that of the municipal district. A- part from that, it seemed to him only a fair and reasonable thing, that the borough should be ex- tended right up to the canal, and ha did not feel that the Rural Sanitary Authority would offer any opposi- tion to that portion of the Bill, and he did not think they, as a Board of Guardians, would disapprove of it. With regard to the mass of houses that had grown up in the direction of Liverpool-road, Winwick-st., and in other directions, it seemed to him that it was a very convenient thing, and conducive to good local adminis- tration that a district of that kind should be conscli- dated for the purposes of local government. Whether there ought not to be clauses of an equitable character, in view of the future rating and liability, in order to re- move any objection that might be felt on that score by the people who owned and lived in those houses was a question rather for the inhabitants themselves than for a public body like a Board of Guardians. But when the borough proposed to go a material distance outside the district he had named—when they proposed to include a material portion of Orfcrd and some portions of Pal- gate, then he thought thei, might, both as a Rural Authority and as a Board, fairly put their foot down and say—" You are going too far." Speaking 'as a county councillor, he might say that the question of the ' extension of boroughs was a very important one throughout Lancashire. There seemed to be a &sire, wisely or unwisely he could not say, to

SEPARATE WARRINGTON FROM TUE COXINTY of Lancaster and to set it up as a county borough, and probably after the rp.xt census wes taken and the new districts conceded, Warrington will be entitled to ask to be converted into a county borough. The rateable value of the borough might be put down at £140,000 or 1 £150,000, and looking at that alone it would be a mere fleabite to the great county of Lancaster, but it was the great extension of boroughs that was being sought all sound that made up altogether a rateable value , of very great importance. He himself thought it a deplorable thing that changes of that kind should involve such

-TREMENDOUS LEGAL COSTS. In Bolton he noticed that a preliminary inquiry, that had been made for the sake of saving the great expense of going before Parliament, was said to have cost no less than £lO,OOO. (" Shame.") The bill of the Rural Sani-1 tary Authority of Bolton was alone £2,000. It was a state of things that was discreditable to the country, and which should not exist amongst intelligent people, 1 when they could net settle a simple question of borough and county areas without involvinF, the ratepayers in so fearful an expenditure as seemed inevitably to accom- pany every one of those inquiries. His own opinion was, with regard to the extensim of Warrington, that they should approach the question from the point of view that it was desirable to come to an amicable arrangement. He thougbt the borough were entitled to I an extension so as to include parts of the Ship Canal; I they were entitled to consolidate the masses of buildings that immediately surrounded the town and to go to al reasonable distance beyond that, but there they should I stop. He had some reason to believe that, if that was brought before the Corporation in the spirit it should be bronght, they would abandon some part of their present scheme, and would be willing to confine the extension to something like the parts he had ventured to sugg,est: (Hear, hear.)—One or two members of the Board expressed their pleasure that the Clerk had brought the subject of the extension of the borough before thorn as he had done, but no discussion took place.

THE great English poet who died in Brow Works. Venice the other week, might fit- tingly have been buried in :Italy, for Italy is essentially the land of song. It is in Rome that the remains of KEATS and of SHELLEY lie, Whilst those of ROBERT BROWNING'S famous wife, Elizabeth BARRATT BROWNING, are interred At ilerenee. If Italy is the poorer, ;Westminster Abbey is the richer by the transference of the remains to England. It is the illustrious 'home of our illustrious dead, and there are none who Will say that lustre is not added to it by the inter- ment within its walls of ROBERT BROWNING. All lasses were so largely' represented at the funeral, mi Tuesday, as to suggest that the poet was Wide of the mark when ho spoke of the "British Mlle, ye who love me not." But there was time when BROWNING was dismissed by the as an obscure versifier who had little 7„• Say and who said that little badly. rt at was long) long ago ; and when he died eollld truly be said of him in the words of Frederic Harrison—" Few men had more riemis, fewer enemies, more devoted admirers." 44`3, yet it cannot -be affirmed that BROWNING is a P°l)taler poet, nor that he is likely to become 171• 2411ar- His meaning seldom lies on the surface; k; is subtle and profound; and there is every- Where evidence of thoughts crowding each _other for expression in such a way that expression oftentimes becomes imperfect. He is as strong salici as deep as Tennyson ; but ho has not Tenny- ee.s self-control andl innate love of the music of words • "Paracelsus" was written half a century -g°, and no one need profess to be surprised that, to n'ing from a comparatively unknown writer, it vlnade no stir in the reading World. It is in blank rse ; it is disquisitions], and it is sometimes °L'aeure. Yet there are scores of lines in the work Which reveal the master-singer. How daring and ,°OW noble in him to say : the So vereiga proof That we devote ourselves to God is seen In living just as though there were no God ! h'le superficial church-goer will be shocked, per- Pso with-the first thought which the words con- ey;\ hut let him dwell upon the passage, and he °ill perceive that it involves the deepest reverence arid the highest religion. Again : There is an inmost centre in us all _Where truth abides in fulness, and aro,ind, Wall upon wall, the gross flesh hems it in, Th This perfect clear perception, which is truth. the is a SHAESPER,EAN ring in these lines, and IS a SHAKESPEREAN way, too, of aptly and There expressing a philosophical conception. inuere has been a good deal said of late about giv- , g the people what is Styled "equality of omen. , • L,3r ; but we have the same idea in this poem Written when BROWNING was a young man. He says:--

But elevate the race at onlefeak! e nvvoemaoskre giants, God! To put just forth our strength, our human strength All starting fairly, all equipped alike. Gifted alike, all eagle-eyed, true-hearted— See if we cannot beat thy angels yet ! IsTo human aspiration has surely gone higher than this; it is the language of a poet who lives for the elevation of the masses even when he does not express himself in the language of the masses. It is as a poet that he feels himself in harmony with nod; for does he not suLlimely say P

Goa is the Perfect Poet, , w Who in creation acts his own conceptions. e have made these brief extracts by way of sug- 4eet2ng that there is much that is elevating and il4lBPiring in one of the earliest and least under- 'heed of BROWNING'S works. He is a poet who elust be judged as a whole rather than by detached Pieees—if justice is to lie done to him; and we eannot but think he would become widely known etld better liked if there were issued a fairly cheap etdition of his works. If his publishers Lre alive to Ivi!? Iligna of the times, they must know that it ld Pay them. If BROWNING is to become popu- hie Poems must be accessible to the people.

Muzzling THE new Board of Agriculture has Dogs. got to work, and is making itself felt in a way which will .be the ..reverse of agreeable to dogs and men, if not to "gods and men." Dog owners are called upon to keep their animals muzzled when they are in any public place. The order came in force with the first day of the New Year, and it is to remain in force until a 'further order is issued. It will be I seen from the notices which have appeared—and one which appears in our present issue—that the regulation is not merely a local one; it is of a , very wide character, so that there will be no escap- ing its operation by passing out of one township into another. The object of the order is to stamp out rabies, if possible; and that it .is possible is a belief which is held by high authorities who have, made a special study of the question. hydro- phobia is such a terrible disease, and results in such a horrible death that the State may well be exercised in taking meastires to reduce its ravages toa minimum. It is no use , de•aling with the disease in a spasmodic and half-hearted way, as has been' done hitherto, one district enforcing a mutzling order, whilst another has no order at all. If any real good is to be done, it must be done by a movement which is operative throughont the country and for a considerable period. There are people who say that muzzling dogs will 'tend to excite aacl increase rabies ; but that is not the pre- valent opinipn ; and, if there be a doubt upon the subject, the matter will probably be determined by ,an edict which is universal in its application. An offender against the order is liable to a penalty of £2O; and authority is given for the seizure, deten- tion and disposal of stray dogs, and of • dogs • not muzzled. There is, however, a glaring exception ; for the order does not apply to dogs while being exercised or used for sporting purposes. This is an impudent, piece of class legislation against which all classes should protest. Hydrophobia may cOme and go,but hunting must go on forever. Common men and 'common dogs may be put to inconvenience by Mr. CHAPLIN*E order; but sport- ing men and sporting dogemust be allowed to go about:at their own sweet will. Such is the view taken by a Department which has a sporting Squire for its chief. As soon as Parliament meets, Mr. CHAPLIN will doubtless be taken to task for this absurd distinction; and meantime the law must be obeyed.

"Tie No one who is familiar with news- Warrington paper matters in Warrington will Advertiser." be surprised to learn that " The Warrington Advertiser" has ceased to exist; for it has been known for some time that it was in a languishing,, not to say moribund, condition. There is not room for two Conservative newspapers in the town; and for some reason or other the Con- servatives of the borough have treated the "Advertiser "as if its existence was of no moment to them. Mr. PowLsoN, the editor and proprietor of what we must now speak of as the late journal, bade adieu to his readers, on Saturday last, in the following terms TO OUR FRIENDS AND SUBSCRIBERS. For nearly Twenty-eight Years we have striven to promote Protestant Conservative principles, and this desire continuing, we shrink now from saying anything which might be made injuriously to affect our country's highest interests. But failing health and resources pre- venting a:continuance of our journalistic efforts, we announce, and naturally with regret, the Discontinuance of the " Warrington Advertiser. ' With very grateful acknowledgments of the kindness ot those .who have ,consistently encouraged us as advertisers, subscribers, and readers, we now, with heartfelt emotion, say— FAREWELL! ' TITE EDITOR. This farewell is brief, but it is suggestive, and it is pathetic. He would be a brute indeed who could be other than sorry to hear of an honourable opponent being compelled to retire through "fail- ing health and resources," and that Mr. powtsori has at all times been an honourable opponent it is a pleasure to us to testify. He has shown him- self alike able and courteous in advocati4 his views; and he has at the same time been and consistent. Indeed, we are afraid it will be said by Churchmen who differ from him, that he has been too rigid for the times. fie is a Conserva- tive of the old school, and, as his Conservatis\m is not a garment that can be altered to suit the altering times, he has been left, so to speak, some- what out oflashion. It is not to be denied that he has served the Conservative party faithfully in the past, and the„leaders of that party owe him a debt of gratitude which ought to be acknowledged now that the journal he has so long conducted is amongst thE things that were. We wish Mr. PowisoN, in his retirement, may have an easier time, improved health, and long life.

John Morley has been postponed, in consequence of the, receipt of it communication from that gentleman intimating that he cannot possibly attend on the date (Jan. 27th) originally s'tlected. No new arrangements have yet been made, but the Com- mittee have matters under their consideration.. Pgraotuum Oth.-3. S. Garland, 51, Bridge-street, War- rington'.—Advt. FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.

- Mr. W. T. IL Husband, deputy-coroner, held an inquest at St. Helens, on the body at George Dixon, aged thirteen years,of Parr Stocks-road, a, pony driver in the Sherdley Colliery, who was killed in the Potato° Deiph Mine, on Monday. Mr. 11.1. Hall, Government Inspector of Mines, was present. Deceased was taking two boxes of coal from the working place to the shunt. He sat on the front box and directed the pony. On reaching the level he ought to have stopped and unhooked the pony. But in jumping off he was knocked down and run over, and died immediately.---A verdict of "Acci- dental death " was returned. CRITORLEY, High Class Tailor, Bold-st. Warringten.---Adyt,
"TOUCH ANI)
There has been an extraordinary rise in scrap steel ; pity if it should, by becoming a precious metal, tempt someone to steal scrap.
Lord Salisbury is said to be indisposed. But this is scarcely news ; he has, for a long time been indisposed—to do anything for the country. Why doesn't he " reform "

"A New York telegram says the Supreme Court, has pronounced the proposed execution of Ketnmler by electricity to be constitutional." The point of law settled, they will soon settle the criminals. Our American cousins have had a long practice at killing people by electricity.

At Newton, and at Daresbury, bread-dealers have been fines for selling bread without weighing it according to law. The clever housewife aims at making light bread; but when she has to buy it she needs to be assured it is 'tot "light." Singular, isn't it? but it is so.

Sir Edward Watkin is about to introduce the Channel Tunnel Bill again. B e has put a lot of plant down, but he is not to be put down himself, for he "bobs up serenely" every year. He must .mind what he is about, or the tunnel rsay becobie "a great bore".

There are all sorts of ways of flooring people— repeating rifles, hundred-ton guns, &c. The latest invention is a new form of influenza. It comes from Russia, and it has already placed thousands hors de combat. Good old Russia! Only please don't let the influenza, like the rifle, become a "repeater."

The Cruelty to Children's Act has been brought into operation at St. Helens. A woman named Elizabeth Smith was sent to prison for two months on Monday, for, illtreating her child. It was proved that she had starved, beaten and even kicked an infant of twelve months old. Such an unmotherly mother deserves all the punishment that prison life will bring her.

thoughtful letter from Mr. E. Whitham will he found on another page. In private note to the editor, dated Dec. Bth, he says :—" Since writing the enclosed, an affair of some importance has. come off. My daughter, Mrs. A. C. Du Nevant, has introduced a son to this world of ours." As the "grandfather" says nothing to the contrary, it may be presumed that mother and child are doing well."

Those who missed hearing "The Lady Whistler" at the Warrington Public Hall, on Monday, missed a treat. The audience was enthusiastic, and the lady was obliging; she gave .more and more. Goldsmith said of Garrick that- 1-le cast off his friends as a huntsman his pack, For he knew, when he pleased, he could whistle
them back. And no wonder, if he could whistle at all like Mrs. Alice Shaw.

Thomas ; Clarke, who was brought beforo the Warrington magistrates,. on Saturday, seems to have been a wholesale t Onveyor of other people's goods. He was convicted' of taking two pairs of men's trousers from one shop,' and a carcase of mutton from another He took,in fact, more than was good for him, and has been sent to gaol for six months, where he will learn, perhaps, "to labour and to wait.'

The Coercion Act is a villainous Act, but the worst of it is that stupid and incompetent Resident Magistrates have administered it most villianously. The " Residents " do not, novvever, have it all their own way. On Thursday Judge Waters, on appeal, quashed three convictions. Two of them were sentences against editors, who were being sent to prison for inserting such news as appears every week in the newspapers of this country.

The other case was that of a farmer; and his Honour, in dismissing him, paid the Crimes Court had no more right to hold the man to bail than they had to hang him. So staggered was the gaoler at being told to set the farmer free, that he asked the judge for a written order, which led to the remark that the gaoler would himself have to go to prison if he did not obey his instructions. Poor gaoler! And how unfortunate it is that "the fiesidents " cannot be put on a plank bed for their stupidities, which are innumerable

The enthusiastic celebrations of Mr. Gladstone's Eightieth Birthday are a healthy sign. Character counts; the Liberal leader is revered not only be- cause he is a great, but because be is a good mall. The" Times further degraded itself—if further degradation is possible—by sneering at the flood of messages which poured into Hawarden on Sun- day aneMonday. The " Times" is very much out of joint ; it is unspeakably mean; A hasn't a soul above Pigott.

Mr. Aaron of the Runcorn Board of Guardians is the gem 9f the collection; but he is not a polished gem. He made offensive allusions, at a recent meeting, to Runcorn jurymen who had simply done their duty ; and on Tuesday he said it was all very well for a certain number to " sit and gabble and write to the newspapers." Mr. Aaron was not knocked ,down ; he was pulled up. Street Arabs have a way at times of saying--" Keep your hair on !" But we shoulrl rather say to the voters at the next election—" Don't keep your Aaron !"

What was described as a whitewash meeting was held at Crewe, on Thursday night; but it didn't wash. The object was to exculpate the railway works officials in the matter of the charge of political intimidation, but the opposition was so great that the resolution could not be carried. A meeting twice the size was held the same night at which it was determined, amid great enthusi- a.srn, to persevere in the exposure of the persecu- tion of Liberal workmen. The directors have fought shy of an inquiry; but the country is be- coming a court of inquiry, and thus far the directors an their Tory underlings stand condemned.

The Clerk to the Warrington Board of Guar- dians has a habit of relieving his mind by dropping nto a speech—just as "Silas Wegg ' used to drop into poetry.' He spoke, on Tuesday, on the Bill which the Warrington Corporation are promot- ing; and remarked that the Town Council "did not impart that degree of information to the rate- payeis which would be useful and proper?' There is a good. deal of truth in this; but it is a way they have in Warrington. The ratepayers are only taken into account just' before the November elections—and not much then. Perhaps the rate- payers will wake up some day, and "want to know, you know."

How they did swear ageneration ago! Anent i Mr. Gladstone's article n the "Nineteenth Cen- tary," the " Star " says:—" Here is one pf the numerous 'damning' stories told of Melbourne, taken from the Ossington papers :—‘ Lord Ossing- ton used to relate that, encountering Lord Mel- bourne when about to mount his horse at the door of the office he called' his attention to some required modifications in his new Poor Law Bill. Lord Melbourne referred him to his brother George. " I have been with him,' was the reply, "but he damned me, and damned the bill, and damned the paupers." "Well, damn it, what more could he do ?';' was the rejoinder."' language is obsolete amongst politicians now-a- days ; they never—that is hardly ever—use "a big big D." I

We cannot afford to give free " advts." ; but we make an exception in favour of the following from the "Church Times ": Advowson for Sale, beautifully situated in Berkshire, near the river ; net income about £3OO • excellent house and grounds ; small pop.., near a station ; incumbent aged nearly 80. It should be understood that "small pop." has no reference to champagne or even ginger beer ; it means" small population "—that is to say there is plenty to get and little to do. FOOTBALL _MATCH AT WIDNES.

About twoMileusand spectators gathered on Widnes football groundcon Nevi Year's Day, to Witness a match between home team and Barrow. , The game was very evenly and stubbornly contested. In the first ,half Morris scored for Widnes, and just before the call df time Cowell scored for Barrow ; the game ending in a draw of one fry each.

div.head: FUNERAL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FUNERAL AT RUNCORN.

On Sunday there were c ,nveyeal to their last resting place, at Runcorn Cemetery, the remainsof Mrs.Lydiate, of Church-st., who had succumbed to her bedil) ai- mnts at the advanced age of 78 years. The body was followed to the grave by Mr.. John Lydiate, the son. and a large number of the tradesmen of the town, and the deacons and members of Bethesda Chapel, with which the deceased lady.was connected. The first portion of the burial service was carried out in the chapel, whence the funeral cortege started. The officiating minister was the Rev. J. W. Bowman, of Lancashire Congrega- tional College. . MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, Ringtopnx. The annual tea party was held on Tuesday evening, when about 130 persons sat down, their wants being attended to by Mesdames Abel, Williams. Cropper, ! Dykes, Mather, and Holmes ; and the Misses Taylor and ! Hill. After tea an entertainment was given, under :he , presidency' of Mr. J. W. Lightburn. Amongst three who - took part in the entertainment were Miss 'Taylor, Miss Hatnpson, Miss McClean, Miss Ada Leithwood, Mips Fleetwood, Misses Worthington, • Miss Holland, Mrs. Thomas, Messrs. E. Wynne Humphreys, R. Morris, Lan- caster and R. Pierooint. On the proposition of Mr. Allen, seconded by Mr. W. Shaw (the Missionary). a vote of I thanks was accorded to the donors of presents for the Christmas tree.—Mr. J. Meadowcroft moved, and Mr. R. Wilson seconded. a vote of thanks •to the Chairman and to those who had provided the entertainment. On Wednesday evening about 270 children were regaled with a capital tea, and were afterwards each presented with an article from the Christmas tree by Mr. R. Abel. After- wards the Rev. T. Patrick (chaplain), spoke a few encouraging words to the children. Mr. R. Abel was thanked for his kind services and at the conclusion of the proceedings, Mr. Shaw asked the children to attend Sunday school regularly. . .

WESLEYAN SALE OF WORK AT WIDNES. With a view to reducing the debt of £250 on Victoria- road Chapel. incurred through the renovation and altera- tion of that building sonse months ago, a sale of work was held in 'Lacey-st. school, on New Year's Day. The opening ceremony was'performed by Mr. T. Robinson. who referred to the spread of Methoaism in the district. In declaring the sale open, he handed over a bank note tr, a donstion.—Mr. B. Brown proooseska vote of thanks to Mr. Robinson, of whom he spoke in eulogistic terms. He held in his hand, he said, a cheque for the clearance of the debt on Moss Bank Wesleyan Chapel. For 17 years that place of worship had struggled, and it had often been recommended to close it, but the members had persevered, and Mark Johnson and Henry Hartley had pulled it through. The prospects were now fairly promising. Mr. E. Davies seconded the vote of thanks, which was carried unanimously, and the sale proceeded. There were two stalls, one from the ladies' sewing class, in charge of Mrs. T. Law ; and one from the Sunday School, which was under the control of Miss Brown, Mrs. D. Davies, and Miss Ward. The Christmas Tree was in care of Miss Poulson, who was assisted by Mrs. W. Taylor and Misses Ward and Hudson. The refreshment stall was presided over by Mrs. Brown and Mrs. Spencer. Various amusements were provided for visitors.

SHOCKING SUFFOCATION CASE AT WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Queen's Arms, Moor-lane, Widnes, on Thursday, touching the death of Andrew Moran, aged 27 years, who had rosided at Hough Green Cottages, Ditton.—Charles Machin, labourer, Halewood, said on Monday, he and the deceased were employed at a thresh- ing machine on Mr. Kelsall's farm. After leaving work in the evening they, together with four other men, went to the Horns Inn and had tvvo half gallons of beer. After- wards they went to the Griffin Inn, Farnworth, where the aeceased had three glasses of rum. He and the ' deceased left that Inn at ten o'clock,when the latter was too drunk to walk home. Witness obtained assistance and took him as far as the Brewery.—A man named Feeney now came up and they put the deceased in a shed adjoining Kelsall's farm and left him.—John Kelsall, farmer, Lowerhouse farm, deposed to finding the deceased in his shed on Tuesday morning. He was ' covered with chaff to the depth of six or seven inches. His mouth and nostrils were filled with chaff ,and he was ' quite dead. There was no doubt the deceased was suffocated. It was a dangerous practice for anyone to lie down in a heap of chaff to go to sleep." The chaff had been trampled down, and either the deceased had covered himself up with the chaff or someone else had.— Thos. Feeney said he was a foreman at a Widnes Chemical work.. Ile was going home between ten and eleven o'clock on Monday night, when he saw a man lying on the rbad near Mr. Kelsall's farm. After much. trouble he roused the man, but found he could not walk, and witness dragged.him into a shed, and placed him on some chaff. He placed some chaff on the man's legs, but did not cover his head at all. By a juryman : He did not see Machin at all. The man was very drunk, and he thought it better he should lie under cover than on tho road.—The Coroner said Feeney did the best he could under the circumstances. There was no doubt Machin had endeavoured to help the deceased home, but if .Feenev was speaking the truth then Machin undoubtedly told a.' falsehood when he said* put the deceased into the shed. He was inclined to believe Feeney. The jury had to conSidcr how the deceased became covCred with chaff.—Thejury returned a verdict of " Aczidoutally suffocated."

div.head: MINERS WAGES.
div.p: MINERS WAGES.

In accordance with the arrangement made be- tween the Lancashiril- and Cheshire Miners' Fe,dern- tion and the St. Helens colliery proprietors, the advance of 10 per cent. in the wages of the miners should have commenced on Wednesday, but as the men were celebrating the advent or the New Year by a holiday the advance will date from Thursday. The advance means that an additional £3OO per week will go 'into the pockets of the men in the borough of St; Helene. ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALE now on. J. &W. Dutton, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

EwELLis, M.P. Information was recently received that Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., who was on a tour with Mr. Brunner, ' M.P., in Upper Egypt, has had a mild attack of fever, and telegrams have since been received announcing that he i• progressing favourably. He-is under the care of an English`doctor at Luxor, and is attended by an English nurse from Cairo. It is understood that Mr. Brunner, M.P., having heard at Cairo that his son was getting better, has returned to Mr. Ellis at Luxor.

ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALE now on. J. 8; W. Dutton, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adat. DOGS AT LARGE : A SINGULAR. CAM At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Col. George McCotquodele"and Messrs, T. J. Gilles- pie, A. C. McCorquodale, IV. P. Gooch and T H. Pearson, George Appleton of the Railway Hotel, Earlestown, was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large and unmuzzled on the ilth December. ' The defendant pleaded guilty. It was stated that the dog was found at the Vulcan, about a mile , away. It was seized by the police, and after being detained three days without the owner being ascer- tained it was sold under the Rabies Order. After it had been so disposed of, the defendant claimed the dog and the Police regained possession, refund- ing to the purchaser the money he had paid for it. The Bench fined the defendant Is. and costs.—Wm. Ellam, Newton, was also summoned for allowing his dog to be at large and unmuzzled on the 18th Dec., and was tined Is. and Costs. MANTEL PIECES in enamelled slate.—Garland. Warrington and Barlestown.—Advt.

div.head: FARNWORE TEMP, ERANCE SOCIETY.
div.p: FARNWORE TEMP, ERANCE SOCIETY.

The annual tea party and entertainment in connection with the Farnwoith branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held in St. Luke's Schoolroom on Wednesday. The subsequent proceedings were pre- sided over by the Rev. J. Roger Jones, 8.A., curate-in- charge. A programme was gone through by the follow- ing artists :Miss Ada Robinson (St. Helens), Miss Haddock, Miss Pritchard, Mr. H. Thewlis (St. Helens), Mr. J. R Lea, and Mr. A. G. Davies. Pianoforte solos were given by Misses 'liner and Hurter, and Miss Haddock and Mr. Thewlis acted as accompanists. INFLICTING GRIEVOUS BODILY HARM AT RUNCORN.

At the Cheshire adjourned Quarter Sessions, held at Knutsford on Wednesday, George Rowson was charged with unlawfully and maliciously inflicting upon William Jolley grievous bodily, harm, at Runcorn, on October 22nd. Mr. Colt Williams prosecuted. it was alleged that the prisoner belaboureacomplainant with a- crutch, inflicting severe wounds abTut the head and other parts of the body. The jury found him guilty on the second cOunt,namely, of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and he was sentenced to two months'imprisonment. ALLEGED THEFT BY AN UNCLE AT WIDNES.

John Conroy, of Skelsmersdale, was brought pp at Widnes Police Court, on MOnday, charged with stealing a coat, value 15s , the property of Patrick Fallon, carter, of 17, Ellison-st., Whines. The prisoner is the uncle of Fallon, and on the 23rd December he was in Widnes on a visit to the latter's parents: On the 24th, he prisoner went with Fallon to the stables and there assisted him to harness the horse, &c., and they left together. The coat was in the stable, but in the evening Fallon was unable to find it. Evidence was given shriwing that the prisoner met a woman named Mrs. Campbell; and asked her to pledge the coat for Bg., and she did so at Carrot's shop in Widnes-rd. The prisoner, who denied, the charge was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALF: now on. J. 8; W. Dutton, Sank ey-st., Warrington.—.Adrt. SUPPER TO RAILWAY MEN AT WIDNES.

On Saturday evening about 50 of the engine drivers and stokers in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company at Widnes, sat down to an excellent supper at the Central Hotel. The good things had been provided from a consolidated fund of Christmas gifts to the employes of the company, by the manufac- turers of the town. Mr. R. Turnbull, foreman of the locomotive department, was voted to the,chair, and Mr. Carter, inspector of the goods department, to the vice- chair. The Chairman remarked that this was the ninth annual gathering they had had through the kindness of the manufacturers, and he hoped they would all be spared to take part in those of years to come. After the loyal toasts had been honoured, the vice-chairman proposed the directors and managers of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and Mr. McConnell, stationmaster, suitably responded.—Mr. Michael Ford gave" The town ana trade of Widnes," and Mr. C. Stringerrepliecl,retuarking that trade was in a flourishing condition.—Other toasts were also honoured, and the proceedings were enlivened with songs, rendered by Messrs. J. Topping, J. Roberts, Joseph Evans, J. E. Bassett, James Lewis;q: R. Lee, F. Grundy, F. Thomas, Wilkinson, Davies, Atkinson, MeNeivin, and Hoskie. SELLING CIGARS WITHOUT A LICENSE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Joseph Snape Eccles. of Windle Grange, St. Helens, was summoned for selling fa quantity of cigars without a license, at Widnes, on the 22nd of October last. Mr. Spencer, supervisor, prosecuted on behalf of the Excise author- ities, and Mr. Swift, St. Helens, defended, and said on behalf of his clienthe admitted the offence.—Mr. Spencer said Mr. Eccles was duly licensed to sell tobacco on cer- tain premises in St. Helens, hut the license did not allow him to sell tobacco anywhere than on licensed premiees. The Offence was simply that Mr. Eccles had sold tobacco away from his licensed premises, and in having shown his goods and then sold them at once to the purchaser, which under the Act constituted the offence. They were endeavouring to nrotect the large duty in tobacco, and prevent the article being hawked, which serionslyaffected the revenue. They did not wish to press the ease against the defendant so much as to give publicity to the terms of the Act.—Mr. Swift said he did not intend to call anftvitnesses, but he might say that on the day in question his client was in the Central Hotel, where he produced his samples, which he was allowed to carry. One of the company wanted to buy one of the sample boxes, and his client, without any thought, sold one to him, He, however, submitted that Mr. Eccles would receive sufficient punishment if he was simply ordered to pay the costs of the case.—Mr. Spencer raising no objection, the Chairman said they were agreed to inflict only a nominal penalty, and to show that it VMS only nominal the fine would be Is. and costs, or in all lie. READ the wonderful! discovery on page 4.—Advt. WHOLESALE SHOP-LUTING AT RUNCORN. At the Cheshire adjourned Quarter Sessions, held at Knutsford on Wednesday, Sarah Pettifer, 65, and Mary Tickle, on bail, were indicated for stealing at Runcorn, en October 15th. articles of drapery, valued at 7s. 6d., the property of David Henry Jones. draper, 57, High-st., Runcorn. Mr. Burke Wood prosecuted, and Mr. E. H. Lloyd represented Tickle. Pettifer pleaded guilty.—A verdict of "Not guilty "was given in the case of Tickle. —The same prisoners were further chkrgecl with stealing two cardig n jackets, value £l. 35., belonging to Jabez Unsworth and Company, clothiers, High-st.. on the same date.—Pettifer said she did not take the jackets, but Mrs. Tickle did.—The jury, after a long deliberation, found both prig niers guilty, and Pettifer was committed to prison for six months, and Tickle for two months.— Sarah Pettifer, along with Selina Faulkner, of no fixed occupation, was then charged with stealing, at Runcorn, on October 12th, two shawls, two skirts, a pair of drawers, and a black dress, the property of William Craddock, pawnbroker, Church-st. William Henry Craddock, son of prosecutor, would not undertake fo swear that the goods in question had never been sold, consequently the case fell through.—Sarah Pettifer, Selina Faulkner, Mary Tickle, and Sarah I3eamer were then &dieted for stealing in the same town,from May Ist to August 29th, a quantity of wearing apparel, &c., the property of Mrs. Walter King. Before the case had proceeded far it broke down under similar circumstances to the last. Particulars of the cases have previously bean published.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHITIICH, WIDNES. The teachers of the Sunday school in connection with this chapel held their annnil tea party, on Tuesday even- ing. About 50 persons were present,and a very pleasant evening was spent.

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The members of this chapel held their annual tea party on Wednesday evening. Afterwards a meeting was held, and severa4 questions affecting the welfare of the church were discussed.

SINM'S CROSS PRIMITIVE METRODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. A social gathering took place in this chapel, on New Ydar's.Day. There was a capital attendance. The pro- ceedings commenced with a tea, and afterwards games, &c., were indulged in for the remainder of the evening.

NEW YEAR'S DAY AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN. New Year's Day was bright and-fine,though very cold, and the majority of the tradesmen's shops were closed. i The works were n full operation as usual. The custom- ary watch night Services were held at the Churches and chapels. ME CHURCH ARMY AT RUNCORN. Captain Wilson, who has been in charge of the Run- corn Branch of the Church Army since its formation,- has been transferred to Northwich. He took his farewell on Thursday evening, whenifa ,meeting, was Add in the rooms in High-st. - - --• '

COM-WM-Sr. WESIMAN MISSION SCIIOOL, WIDNES.• On Tuesday evening about 150 children attending this mission were entertained to tea and afterwards an enter- tainment was held under the presidency of Mr. John Hargreaves.. In the course of the proceedingn fruit was distributed amongst the juvenile audience. •

s NEWSBOYS' TREAT AT WIDNES. A lar;-4-0 number of the newsboys of the town had their annual treat, on New Year's Day, at the residence of 'Mrs. Morewood, Widnes-rd. The cog of the treat was defrayed by subscription, and the boys were given a sub -tantial tea, and were afterwards regaled with fruit, &c. The evening was spent In games and music.
WIDNs'C.E.T.S.

Mr. and Mrs. Farrant, on Monday evening provided the members of the Band of Hopei with their annual tea, and the young people', spent a very happy time.—On Thursday evening Mr, R. A. Naylor, of Warrington, de-- liverect a lecture to the members of the 'society, on the subject of "General Gordon. There. was a good at- tendance, and the Vicar presided. . A WIDNFAI,MAN DROWNED AT LIVERPOOL. About half-past severe on Saturday night John Edwards, aged 34, belonging to Widnes, while working on board a flat in the Coburg Dock, fell down a ladder on to a dredger and again off the latter into the water. Ilia wife was standing near him, and gave an alarm; but, although several policemen were speedily on the spot with grappling irons, his body was not recovered until nine on Sunday morning. ANNUAL CLEARA.NCE, SALE now on. J. A W. Dutton, •Sankey-st.. Warrington.- Advt. • CHRISTMAS. TREE AT WIDNES NATIONAL SCHOOL. The annual Christmas tree for the children attending the Parish Sunday School, was held on New Year's Day, and the event passed off very successfully. The proceed- ings were opened by. the Vicar in an appropriate manner, and the 250 children who were present enjoyed them- selves to the full until late in the evening. The Christmas tree was stripped of its load of toys, Sze., and a variety of games were allowed those present. • ' '
A Win iCES FAIL' mus.

At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Thursday, tipfore Mr. Registrar Bellringer, Thomas Basnett, who was'a journeYman cooper at Widnes, and had a small fancy goods shop at Appleton,. in Widnes, came before the court for public examination with a statement, of affairs showing. liabilities £lB7, and assets nil. The bankrupt was ordered to file a deficiency account, and the examination was adjourned to January 16ch..

DE.tm ov Mits. WAss, or Runcorn:. Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mrs. Was, wife of Mr. W. R. Wass, of the Wellington Hotel, who is a, member of the Board of Cormnissioners. For a considerable pericid'Mrs. Wass had been in a weak state-of health, through an affection of the heart, and a week ag,cr the symptoms were complicated' with conges- tion of the lungs, and her condition became alarming. She breathed her last at an early hour Or. Thursday morning, and her decease will be lamented by a large circle of friends, by whom she was held in the highest respect. Mrs. Wass has attained the age of 41 years.

div.head: TRAP ACCIDENT AT WIDNES„
div.p: TRAP ACCIDENT AT WIDNES„

A lively scene occurred in Widnes-road 'on Thurs- day afternoon. Mr. W. Wood. of Crow Wood. was paying a brief visit to his slaughter, who resides in Gossage-st. He left his horse and trap in charge of a boy and went in the house. From some unex- plained cause the horse, which is a spirited animal, took fright and dashed along the street at a terrific pace, 'and failing to take the corner into Widnes- road, rushed headlong into the window of Mr. A. .T. Loines' furniture shop. The large plate glass" win- dow was smashed to atoms, and sad havoc was played with the hardware goods displayed for sale, while the animal was very badly cut about the head, neck, and legs. The damage to the shop and goods is about £2O.

ST. EDWARDS CATHOLIC SCHOOL, RUNCORN. A large audience assembled in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening, to witness the children in attendance at the schools give an entertainment. The firs', part of the programme consisted of the operetta -.Red Riding Rood," in four scenes. The characters were represented as follows :—Red Riding Hood, Miss Lizzie Whittley; the mother, Miss Maria McKeown ; the wolf, Master J. H. Leigh ; the Woodman. Masters.!. Quinn, J. W. Keogh, and J. Kennedy ; com- panions, Miss Julia lily and 'Miss. Fanny Whittley ; flowers, rose, Miss V., Kennedy, buttercup, Miss I'Maggie Craig. The characters were brightly sus- tained by the young people. Miss Whittley in the prin- cipal part acted and sang with much ability, and was frequently applauded. The Maypole dance was cleverly executed. In the second part the play entitled "The Reverse medal" Was performed,the cast being as follows: Countess Errard, Miss Lizzie Leigh ; Isabel, Countess' daughter, Miss Annie Kennedy; governess, Miss Julia. Reilly ; maid to the Countess, Miss Nellie Kennedy; housemaid, Miss Maria McKeown ; Mother Alarum, Miss Maggie Stanton; Jane, the shepherdess, Miss Lizzie Whittley. The 'humours of the play were well depicted and caused much amusement. The intervals were filled up with songs and recitations. Miss Julia Reilly gave a skipping rope dance in capital style, the infant scholars recited" Christmas Stockings," and gave the recitation "Twelve months of the year," besides singing several choruses ; Mips Nellie Williamson recited "Sulking," and Miss Maggie Redmond sang" I'm the old Woman." A most enjoyable evening concluded with the chorus ". Goodnight "by the assembled children.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on TueAday. Coloncl Alibton presided, and there were present the Rev. J.' W. N. Tanner, Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Stokes, It. Lewis; J. Baguley, J. Brandreth, Mclntyre, Hall, Pickering, Bretnerton, Knowles, IL Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and Farrington (nuisance inspector).
HOW SCARLET FEVER IS SPREAD.

_ The Medical Officer reported a case of scarlet fever in Fleun-lane, Frodsham. At the time of his visit the Auld, who was in the " peeling " stage of the disease, was sitting ,in the living room, surrounded by all it, brothers anc: sisters. Ile remonstrated with the mothers but failed to elicit any distinct promise that she would isolate the child,in accordance with hissuggestions. Such eondithms, he need scarcely point out, were a fruitful source of infection, as the healthy children were allowed access to other children, and the 126th section of the Public Health Act failed to reach such cases. It was cases like these which demonstrated most/le.arly the need for a special hospital for infeetiou4 diseases, coupled with power on the part of the Sanitary Autho- rity, or its officials, to remove the cases, and to keep them isolated until the danger of infection was over. It was most probable that the Authority would soon hear of fresh cases which might be traced to this single case in Fluen-lane.—Mr. Stoles: Were these children attending school ?—Pr. Adams said he did not know, but he told the mother that she had no right to allow them to go to school, but he could not prevent them going into the streets, and playing with other children, and the first child they shook hands with would become infected.— Mr. Stokes said no wonder that scarlet fever spread so long as such a cendition of affairs existed. This was all the business of interest.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided and there, were present the Rey. J. W. N. Tanner- Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Knowles, Lewis Bran- dreth, Jeffs, D. H. Jones, Bretherton, Hall, Pickert ing, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (assistan clerk). THE SCHOOLMASTER'S APPOINTMENT UNSANCTIONED. - _

The following letter was read from the Local Govern- ment Board:—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 18th inst., from which it appears that the Guardians of the Runcorn Union have re-appointed Mr. Thomas Stubbing as schoolmaster at the Workhouse. I am directed to state that having regard to thecircumstances under which Mr. Stubbing resigned his office at the Doncaster Union Workhouse, and to the circumstances which led to his resignation at Runcorn, in October last, the Board would not feel justified in assenting to his again holding office as schoolmaster to the Workhouse.—Signed, Alfred D. Adrian."—Mr. Jeffs said there was no explanation in that letter satisfactory to the Guardians who voted for Mr. Stubbing. He moved that the clerk write to the Local Government Board and ask for a fuller .explanation—Mr. D. H. Jonesseconded the motion. Mr. Stubbing was appointed by 17 votes to 8, and they cught to know as well as the Local Government Board what were the objections to him. The Guardians ought to have the appointment of their own officers, and Mr. Stubbing was appointed on the principle that he had the best credentials. He had earned• Government grants averaging £4B a year, a thing unprecedented in that Union. He had earned £l.O a year morn than wa.s done in any six years previous to his appointment. The Guardians acted honestly by re-appointing Mr. Stubbing, and his re-appointment had given general satisfaction throughout the Union.—Mr. Tanner corrected Mr. Jones, and said the voting was not 17 to eight, but 17 to 13.- -The Assistant Clerk : There were 30 members present and the voting was 17-8-s.—Mr. Aaron said Mr. Jones had a great deal to say about Mr Stubbing earning more grant than any previous master in the house. It would have been a great disgrace to him if he had not because the number of children was inc.rea.sing, and they were constantly at school morning and afternoon, and conse- quently there would be more passes and more grant. It ; would be a 'waste of time to write to the Local Govern-1 ment Board, because they would not sanction his re- ' appointment and what were the Board to do without a schoolmaster in the meantime. It was all very well for such as Mr. Jones to come and sit there and then gabble and write to the papers, but let them attend to I the business of the Board and study matters for the 'benefit of the ratepayers.—Mr. Jeffs asked if the reasons why the schoolmaster left Doncaster were supplied to the Board when he was appointed. —The Assistant Clerk: The Board had great difficulty in getting' the sanction of the Local Government Board to the appointment then, because of the Doneastet4 business.—The Clerk said that letter had only been received that morning and there had been no time to look up the previous appointment.—Mr. Brandreth thought the least said in this matter and the better.—Mr. Mclntyre disapproved of sending the letter proposed,— Mr. Knowles supported the motion because a majority of the Guardians voted for Mr. Stubbings' re-appointment

and it would not be satisfactory unless a full explana- tion was given.—lTltimatelv Mr. Jeffs' motion was lost by nine votes to live.—Mr. Mclntyre gave notice that at the next meeting he should move that Mr. R. S. Gleave be appointed schoolmaster.—Mr. J. Stokes gave notice that he should move the appointment of Mr. Naylor, of Warrington.—Mr. Jeffs gave notice that at the next meeting he should propose that Mr. Stubbing be allowed to commence his duties as schoolmaster to the Work- house, after being elected to the post by the Guardians of the Board (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—MT.Brandreth moved that Mr. Dansey, the Government Inspector, be asked to attend the meeting.—Mr. Aaron seconded, and the motion was carried, and the discussion then ceased. The remainder of the business was not of public in- terest.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD_ OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD_ OF GUARDIANS.

• The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was hefrl t Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, there were present the Rev. Dean Fine- gan (chairman), Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. Fisher, W. Middle- burst, G. E. Chadwick, J. Birchall, W. Davies, J. Peover, E. Ellison, J. Burchall, W. Lowe, E. Syder, C. B. Johnson, J. Ranson, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Mercer, R. A. Graves, J. Marsh, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). INMATRS.—The Workhouse master reported there were 575 inmates this week, 576 last week, and 567 in the corresponding week last year; 51 vagrants had been relieved, against 413 in the corresponding period last year. CHRISTMAS GIFTS:—On the recommendation of the 'Visiting Committee hearty thanks were tendered to the donors oUGhristmas gifts to the inmates. ECCLESTON AND WINDLE TOWNSHIPS.—A. letter was read from the Local Government Board with respect to the property in Ecoleston and Windle townships, and suggesting that the money should be re-invested in 'accordance with a former order of the Board.—Mr. Middlehurst asked if it could not be applied towards the cost of erecting the new relief offices in St. Helens.— The Clerk said it could not.—The subject was referred to the Finance Committee.

UNION LoaNs.—The West Ham Biwa of Guardians wrote seeking the support of the Guardians of Prescet Union to a memorial to the Local Government Board praying that the period of repayment of loans be ex- tended from 30 to 50 years.—lt was decided not to sup- port the memorial. EMIGRATION AND IMMIGRATION.—The Clerk read a letter from the National Association for Promoting State Conolization, which stated that the objects of the Association were to induce the Government to adopt a system_ of state conolization in order to relieve the congested districts and labour markets of Great Britain. The support of the Prescot Guardians was asked.—Mr. Tyrer said he thought they should first prevent immigra- tion into this country before they took any steps in regard to emigration Germans and others were coming over, and insteadof their being a congestion of workmen there was a deficiency in the supply of good workmen.— Mr. Middlehurst agreed with Mr. Tyrer on that matter, and said if anyone wanted to go to Natal, Australia, or any other country there were plenty of facilities with- out the Guardians being in any way responsible.—Mr. Burchall thought our own lands ought to be occupied by, good men instead of sending them out to other countries. —Mr. Ellison moved that the letter lie on the table, and the Chairman in seconding, said he always looked with suspicion on emigration schemes.—The motion was passed. This was the principal business. . ,

div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. CELEBRATION OF MR. GLADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. CELEBRATION OF MR. GLADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.

The first "house dinner' in connection with Runcorn Liberal Club wal' held on Monday evening. in celebration of the 80th birthday of Mr. Gladstone. The newsroom and Committee room had been con- verted into supper rooms, and about 60 guests sat down to the repast provided. Amongst these pre- sent were Messrs. T. Hafelley, J. J. Howitt, R.. Morris, G. Bellamy, J. Jeffs, W. Handlpy, E. Wynne Humphreys, E. Marshall, J. D. Jones, J. Clarke, J. Holt, T. Clegg, J. Unsworth, J. Pritchard, T. Dean, Jepson, E. Taylor, R. Pierpoint, W. Chad- wick, J. Poole, Billington, it. Rawlinson, R. Moore (secretary). Before the diners set to work with their knives and forks Mr. Moore, the secretary, despatched a congratulatory _telegram to Mr. Gladstone by the unanimous desire of those present. After dinner the company assembled in the Committee room, and Mr. T. Handley was unanim- ously voted to the chair. The Chairman said that the members of that club desired to add their congratulations 'to the number Mr. Gladstone had received. Mr. Leathwood then sang, "God bless the Grand Old Man." the •audience joining heartily in the chorus. The Chairman proposed the health of Mr. Brunner, the president of the club, and the toast was received with musical honours.—Mr. W. Handley responded on Mr. Brunner's behalf, and mentioned the • meeting to be held in Runcorn on January 21st. At the request of the Club he had obtained the services of Mr. Stansfield, an eminent speaker and a member of the late Government, a man who on local government matters had no superior in England—as principal speaker. (Applause.) He knew Mr. Brunner,. who would be present himself, would like that meeting to be a great success. Mr. Ellis and Mr. Tomkinson were also expected to be present. Song, Mr. Clegg, "The brave old oak." The next sentiment proposed by the Chairman was "Our local legislatures."—Mr. Marshall was called upon to respond for the Board of Commissioners. After making some allusion to local affairs, he said that Vetoes - was no man to whom we owed more for the condition in which we found ourselves than our grand leader, whom they were met that night to honour. We could sit finder our own palm and fig tree, and none dare to make us afraid. (Applause).—Mr. Jeffs responded for the Board of Guardians, and defended his action on the schoolmaster incident, on the ground that he did not think the man had fair play, and concluded by stating that there was not a better managed workhouse than that of the Runcorn Union.—Mr. Hewitt was called upon to respond for the School Board. There were one or two questions he intended to ask at the School Board, which he hoped would be of benefit to the ratepayers of Runcorn. He would ask them we hout partiality and he hoped without prejudice, and he should have an answer if he could get it. However, he did not suppose there was a single gentleman on the Board who would do a dishonorable act. (Hear, hear.) He had in days gone by eschewed personalities and he always intended to do• iso n politics or local contests. He had seen a good deal of political life, and had fought many political battles, and had it not been for his decided political opinions he should never have been in Runcorn that day, but he would sacrifice anything rather than any man should interfere with his civil and religious liberties. He thought that Liberal Club might be of great service to the young men of Runcorn.—Mr. J. D. Jones replied on beh-alf of the Free Library Committee, and remarked that the Library was doing a vast amount of good in the community. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. Morris sang " The light of other days." The Bev. Charles Garnett proposed "The union of hearts and hands—Home Rule," and said the principle underlying Home Rule was one that was alto- gether fundamental to Liberalism. He meant the• principle of political justice. (Hear, hear.) There were those who thought the question of Home Rule. depended upon the life of Mr. Gladstone. He had. heard that if Mr. Gladstone departed this life thC Liberal party would quickly fall to pieces. This was altogether a misconception as to the spirit of the Liberal party. He was convinced that the Liberal party, having adopted the principles underlyiug Home Rule, would take good care that it should come to the front. —ln responding to the toast, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys uttered seine appropriate sentiments, and went on to speak of local institutions. It appeared to him that they could do a great deal in that club to foster a healthy municipal life. They had a duty to perform, and he for one should be glad to see the members of the Club actively and nobly, according to their various situations and the powers which were in them endeavouring to take their share in the public life of the town. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to the Free Library, Mr. Humphreys said he should be glad to see the Library and news- room open on Sundays for the use of the inhabitants. He thought. it was very hard lines upon the working- men that the only places where they could find any amount of recreation outside the chapels and churches should be the public-houses. As long as these things existed in the.form they did, he should use his voice and influence that a rational means of education should be open to theffi on Sunday, as well as week day. .Mr. Walter Millington recited "God save the People," and Mr. Moore sang the political song "Justice, Truth, and Right."

The 'Chairman then proposed "Our Liberal . Club," and Mr. Moore. in replying, said ha was pleased' to state that although the club had only been in existence about 12 Weeks, they had 184- members on the books. On the first quarter's workinz,af ter paying all ex ptinses.they would have a balance of about £lO in hand. They hoped to have a large accession of members wh.:ll the New Year came in. The club was not formed for recreation merely, but for educational purposes, and if this latter was not attended to, the Club would have failed in the : object for which it was established. (Appiau.;e). Song—" When other lips and other hearts." byMr. Pilgrim. On the proposition of Mr. CLEGG, seconded by 111 r.. RA.wriNsox, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to, the. chairman, and that gentleman having acknowledv,d the compliment, three hearty cheers were given for Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. The proceedings I. onclude.d by singing a verse of the national anthem. BEECHAM S P&L WOt.I(S. •

div.head: MYSTERY OF THE SHADOWS.
div.p: THE MYSTERY OF THE SHADOWS.

One gloomy night in November, 1886, a policeman in the upper part of the City of New York saw the shadows a two persons pass rapidly across the window shades of a house, and then disappear as though the persons had gone to the farther end of the room. As the officer looked, this occurred again and again; ten, twenty, fifty, one hundred times, regularly, about once in thirty seconds. His curiosity was aroused, and he continued to watch. At first the shadows were those of a man and a woman, then of two women, then a man and a woman. Always two shadows, and one always of the same vraman. He heard no sound. Some-time afterwards a letter was published, which explained the midnight ,mystery. The writer said "About three years ago my health, which had pre- viously been good, began to give way. The first sign of it was a Weakness of the digestion with the symptoms -which invariably accompany that common disorder. Instead of passing away, as I thought it would, this trouble grew worse. I called upon our regular family physician, a gentleman of high repute and in large prac- tice, who prescribed for me, and I continued under his care for several months. During the latter part of that time he called almost daily at our house, as I was not able to go out. None of the remedies given seemed to benefit me. The liver was torpid, and there were plain symptoms of a trouble of the kidneys. In the co urse of a few weeks I was seized with acute nervous prostration. For months my sleep had been poor and broken ; now I scarcely slept at all. For more than a week I took no food whatever; the very sight, smell, or thought of it disgusted and upset me. At night I would lie for awhile upon the bed, with the gas burning dimly, and try to go to sleep. It was impossible. My mind was so active and disordered that the figures in the carpet and the wall paper took the shape of hideous faces which appeared to watch me and mock my distresi. I realised that I was on the verge Of mania or insanity, and did not dare to go near a win- dow for fear I might not be able to resist the tempta- tion to jump out and kill myself. Many nights my hus- band and children to oh turns in walking the floor with me when I could neither sleep nor keep quiet in any position.* I was in this terrible condition when Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup was first brought to my notice by an intimate acquaintance who had used it. I said I would take it, of course, but had no faith it would have the slightest effect on such a case as mine. I took a ;lose late that night, and, before morning, I had one hour's solid sleep. I remember I lost myself when the clock was striking two, and awoke again at three. But I was quiet, although wakeful, until morning. From this time I used Mother Seigel's Syrup regularly. The next -effect was to correct the digestion, after which I slept as well as in my childhood. I took no other medicine while making a trial of this one, nor have I since. One day, recently, I counted the prescription bottles brought frprn the chemist's shop daring my illness, and there were forty of them. Some had been filled several times. Besides the cost of the medicine my husband paid a heavy doctor's bill. lam confident that if Mother Seigel's syrup had not been thrown in my way I should now be In an insane asylum or in my grave. (Signed) " Mits. FRANCES Housnoolt, " 440, East, 115th Street, New York." It must not be supposed that there is any opium or Ither narcotic in Seigel's Syrup, for there is not. In Mrs. Ilolbrook's case, as in all others, it produces quiet and -rest by destroying the poisen in the blood caused by in- digestion and dyspepsia. It was this poison going to the brain that brought on the symptoms she so graphi-

cally describes. • It was the husband and daughter of the half-crazed woman walking the floor with her by turns, and passing between the gaslight and the windows, that pazzled the policeman, and led him to think there was something strange and Irregular about the inmates of the house.
