On Tuesday' at the Warrington Police Court. a navy named Joseph Williams pleaded not guilty to a charge of having, on the Bth ult., stolen a quantity of house- kold linen, value 35., the property of John Shaw, land- lord of the Harp and Crown Inn, Irla in-street. Evid- ence was given to the effect that the prisoner visited the beerhouse in company with another man, and im- mediately after they had left the articles were missed. The Bench considered the case a suspicious one, but de- cided to dismiss it.

div.head: DRUNKEN THIEF " CAUGHT IN THI3 ACT."
div.p: A DRUNKEN THIEF " CAUGHT IN THI3 ACT."

A. man who gave the name of Thomas Clarke, and who said that he was a Ship Canal navvy, was before the Warrington magistrates on Saturday, on a charge of having stolen half a carcase of mutton, valued at 21 Zs. 3d. Prisoner, who said that he had been drinking, and did not remember stealing anything. was seen by Constable Monoghan loitering about Bridge-st. When passing the shop of Joseph Shaw, butcher, he took from a hook half a carcase of mutton, and was at once appre- hended by Monoghan and Sergeant Rovrbotham. It was afterwards ascertained that he had stolen a pair of trousers from the shop of Messrs. Robertson and Sons, Buttermarket-St. He was sent to prison for six months, with hard labour, three months on each charge.

AN UNRULY SON IN COMIT. Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a young man named James Sauce was brought up on eharges ot having been drunk and disorderly in Bank- at., on Thursday night, of having assaulted Timothy and Bridget Sauce, and of having committed damage by breaking eleven panes of glass at the house of his father. Prisoner's father said that he was sorry to appear against his son, but he could not help it. Prisomer went home on the night previous, after having sold a pair of boots his mother had bought him on the day before. Because his mother would not give him twopence with which to buy beer, he attacked her, and a struggle ensued in which several members of the family took part. Prisoner after- wards broke eleven panes of glass. It was his sixteenth appearance, and he was fined 20s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment in default of payment.

A CHRISTMAS JOLLIFICATION. A number of people living in the neighbourhood of Smith-street, had a jollification on Christmas Day, at the house of Mrs. Jane Newnes. A considerable quantity of beer was " put down," and one of the guests, when she I went home, took away a shawl that was the property of the hostess. The result was that on Saturday, the per- son in question, the wife of a labourer named Flynn, was charged with stealing the shawl. From the evidence adduced it appeared that on Christmas Day, the prisoner and a number of men and women, to the uumber of about a dozen, were drinking together in the house of the prosecutrix horn closing time at half-past two till eleven o'c!ock at night. Mr. Newnes, feeling tired, went to bed at about eleven, leaving his wife and the prisoner below. Mrs. Newnes at length fell asleep and when she -awoke found herself alone in the house, and the shawl was missing. In answer to questions from the Bench, the prosecutrix said half a crown was spent in the pur- chaseof liquor. About eight half gallons of beer were drunk, and they sang and danced, but did not play at •eards. The,drink was purchased by subscriptions from those present: and they sent for beer till all their money bad been spent. Prisoner, who said the prosecutrix had lent her the shawl, was fined 205., including costs.

DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence John Carroll was fined 58,, including costs; Edward Norman was also fined in the same sum; and Mary Thompson was cau- tioned and dismissed. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Annie Noon was summoned for having assaulted Mary Hughes, on the 26th ult.—The evieence was of a contradictory character, and the Bench dismissed the case.

jun. DRITNYENNESS.—For this offence Peter Hay, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs; Benjamin Shepherd and George Rowlands were each fined ss. and costs; and Thomas Parry was fined ss. and Costa. div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (in the chair), J. Marson, and W.Long. A BREAD DEALER FINED.—John Shaw was fined Ss. and costs for selling bread other than by weight at Appleton on the 4th December to a woman named Eliza Ann Whatton.

• AN OBSTRUCTIVE CART —William Plinston, qf Warring- ton, was summoned for having on the 16th December, at Appleton, left his cart an unreasonable time on the high- way at Appleton, namely for 25 minutes, to the obstruction of passengers.—A fine of 2.5. 6d. and costs was inflicted. ALLEGED Wua ASSAULT.—WiIIiam Davies, described as the tunnel keeper for the North Staffordshire Rtilway Company at Preston Brook, was charged with having on the 16th December assaulted his wife.—Mr. Arthur Linaker was for the complainant, and Mr. Arthur Browne for the defendant.—Mr. Linaker said the complainant was a widow when she married the detend- ant. On the day in question she went to see her daughter at Manchester, and returned about eight o'clock in the evening. The defendant was sitting near the fire. The complainant put down a bag and several parcels, I whereupon the defendant jumped up and told her to " clear out." He then took up the poker,and seeingthat he intended to assault her, she made for the door, and just as she had got between the door and the post the poker was thrown against the door.—Mr. Brown contended that no assault had been proved, and that he had no case to answer.—The Bench dismissed the case.

GAME TRESPASS.—Thomas Fritz, a labourer, was sum- moned for having on the 24th November, at Moore, com- mitted a trespass by entering on the daytime certain land in the possession and occupation of Mr. John Bradbury in search of game, without the license or con- sent of the owner of the land so trespassed upon.— Joseph Jones, gamekeeper in the service of Sir Richard Brooke, proved the case. The Bench fined defendant ss. and costs.

DittflatENwEss.--David Burrows, Thomas Owen, and Samuel Goodier, were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk on the highway, at Little Leigh, on the 22nd December. BREACH OF THE CONTAGIOITS DISEASES (Ammets') ACT. —Robert Brookes, James Brookes, and Thomas Brookes, cattle dealers, Statham were each summoned fora breach of the above Act, Robert for having on the 29th Novem- ber moved five heifers from Warrington to Statham without a license, James for moving one cow and one heifer from Warrington to Thelwall also without a license, and Thomas Brookes for causing five heifers to be moved from Warrington to Statham. The facts of the case were stated by Constable Millington. The two first-named defendants pleaded guilty, but Thomas Brookes denied that he had caused the heifers to be moved from Warrington to Statham. They should have been left on his own land at Latchford. His son was taking them there, but when at Latchford the animals got away from him and strayed to Statham.—The case against Robert Brooks/ was dismissed, James was fined 10s. and costs, 9s. 9d., and Thomas ss. and 10s. 9d. costs.
WIDNES POLIcE COURT. MONDAY.—Before T. S. Timmis. DRUNKENNESS.-6 eorge Flannigan, of Warrington, and John Nolan, of no settled abode, were each lined ss. and costs for drunkenness.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THITRSDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, sen. (chairman), and Holbrook Gaskell, jun. DRIINKENNESS.—Anastasia Burns, Sutton's-lane ; John Crowley, Catherine-st. ; Ephraim Cooper, Mersey-view ; Thomas Kinchley, 37, Cromwell-st. ; Thomas Shone, 9, Luton-st., and George Worth, Hough Green, were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk at Widnes during the Christmas festivities.

BREACH OF THE PBACE.—Ntrick McCabe, Midwood- st., was summoned for causing a breach of the peace at Widnes on the 22nd ult.—The defendant was bound over for three months, himself in £lO and to find two sureties in £5 each.
RUNCORN POLICE COURT. TIIESDAY.—Bef ore Mr. A. Thomas.

_ A PAWNBROKER ROEBED.—Thomas Flepworth, a youth, was brought up on remand charged with stealing al jacket, value 13s. 6d., the property of Harriett Dodd, pawnbroker, on the 23rd December. The circum- stances have been reported. The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days hard labour. AGAIN REMANDED.—Henry Hall and Fergus O'Connor Nugent, strangers, were chlrged on remand with steal- ing a pair of boots,worth ss. 6d., the property of Henry Stone, Church-st. The prisoners were again remanded for further inquiries. TRErESDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. G. L. Wigg. NEW YEAR'S JOLLIFICATIONS.—John Poole. Daniel Devanny, Charles Henry Crawford, and Joseph Shaw, were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly on New Year's Day. Thomas Houghton and John Wright were charged with resisting P.C. Malkin in the execution of his duty on New Year's, Day and a fine of 10s. and costs was imposed upon each defend- ant.

ROBBING THE GIIXEDIANS.—Edward Littlemore, of Frodshatn, a well-known character, was charged with stealing a pair of trousers, value 2s. 6d., the property of Runcorn Guardians. The prisoner had been an inmate of the Workhouse, and had absconded with the trousers. As he was an incorrigible character he was cOmmitted for trial.

THE ASSESSMENT OVERSEER THREATENED AT RUNCORN. —At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Joseph Plant, salt boiler, of King-st., was brought up under a warrant charged with having, on the 23rd December, used threats towards William Sutton, the assistant overseer. Mr. Sutton said he assisted Miss Law to collect her rents, and she had occasion in July to distraitr from the prisoner for rent. The goods did not realise sufficient to pay the whole of the arrears, and there was a balance of 5s 6d. against him. He asked him to settle his rant book, and he told him he could not until the money was paid. On the 23rd inst. the prisoner followed him into several cot- tages, and in a very offensive manner held up his fist, and ,threatened to knock Ws—jaw off. He was afraid the prisoner would do him some bodily harm. The prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months in the usual sureties, and was ordered to pay 114 s, 6d. costs.

div.p: A GIFT OF 1:100,000.

An unknown " founder" has set apart the magnificent sum of £lOO,OOO for the establishment of a convalescent home—such as the noble institution at Cheadle—in con- nection with some of the London hospitals. Sir William Savory, President of the British College of Surgeons, has been requested to act as trustee with the donor in the administration of the fund.

Mr. Gladstone will address a political meeting at Chester on the 22nd inst. The gathering, for which the Music Hall has been secured, will be held in connection with the Chester Liberal Association, a which Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., who will take the chair, is president. RUGBY.

WAERINGTON A. v. BARROW.—This fixture, which is the only one for this season, was played at Barrow on Saturday. The match had been looked forward to witiv considerable interest, this be:ng the first tour for the A team. The team arrived at their destination shortly after one, and after a hasty look round the town, betook themselves to the Barrow headquarters to prepare for the match. Orl arrival at the ground a fair attendance of spectators had assembled, but the field was on the hard side, and several ugly knocks occurred during the game. Barrow winning the toss, Isherwood started up- hill and against a stiffish breeze, and Neild at once took play be the home quarters. Notwithstanding the hard ground, the ball travelled rapidly from end to end, and following some loose work Eyre shoneconspicuously I by a grand bit of play, and mainly through his efforts ' the Barrow quarter was reached. Jones at length brought about relief, and Isherwood immediately after- wards staved a determined rush of the ' opponents at midnelcl. 'Here the game for a time was carried on fierce- ly, until a dribble, started by Isherwood, Eyre, and Davies, caused the home supporters some anxiety. Davies next started soinci nice passing, but Jones subse- quently kicked to touch-near centre. Some more long kickine. between Daniels and Barnett followed, and then J. Bowker ran very strongly to the Warrington lino. A fine dribble, in which Barnes, Beard, and Dillon Were eotable, quickly removed the threatened danger, but some pretty short passing by Haney, Weodend, and Bowker was nipped in the bud by Sampson kicking to the Barrow quarter flag. Immediately afterwards by a spell of good passing and dribbling by Hindle, Haney, and Woodend, the home team seemed sure to score, but Isherwood saved the try, and Boecow kicked to the 25, when Lawless was prominent by a fast follow up. Molyneaux next got nicely away, but his pass, was not taken advantage of, and soon afterwards Daniels relieved finely from a fine rush of the home team. More exchanges followed between the opposing backs, and then Eyre and Nield dribbled beautifully from halt way over the Barrow line, the former gaining a capital try. Isherwood made a fine attempt at goal. The drop out was returned by Holmes. Holmes next dribbled single- handed to the Barrow line, tackling Jones before he could return. Warrington were almost over several times at this stage, Lawless and Mather baffling their opposing halfs by their short passing. Dillon, however, secured a try, although the place failed. Following the drop out J. Bowker effected a fine strong run, and a miskick almost let the Barrow men in. Danger was averted, however, and when the whistle blew for half- time the visitors led by two tries to nil. On resuming at centre Mather was early conspicuous by a run and pass to Sampson, whose kick was well returned by Jones. Bowker next tried to get through, but Davies tackled too surely, and Barrow were agaiu severely depressed. The home team relieved the pressure by intercepting some passing of their opponents, and Bowker put his side on a more advantageous footing by a beautiful bit of play. The game now slowed down somewhat, Davies, Beard, and Molyneux, in the meantime showing up by good play. Give-and-take play ensued, and then a good kick by Sampson was well followed up by Davies and Beard, and the home back mulling the ball Beard had an uninterrupted, walk launder the posts, the place failing. From the drop out Boscow kicked capitally and Jones returning but feebly the home line was again in danger. The visiting forwards here screwed a scrimmage grandly, but a try was averted, a minor only accruing. Soon after the kick out Daniels tackled J. Bowker in fine style, and some nicepassing by Mather. Lawless, and Sampson pressed the home team. Isherwood from a line-out was almost over, but Barrow relieved. Nield then got away grandly, and when near the line threw across to Mather, who easily scored a try. Succeeding the drop-out Lally put in a smart run, and immediately afterwards Hindle saved a dribble by Isherwood. Molyneaux, and Barnes under the posts. After a grand relief by Boscow another try was obtained by Mather, Warrington winning by 5 tries and one minor to nil. Teams.—Warrington Bos- cow, back; Sampson, Daniels, and Lally, three-quarters; Mather and Lawless, half backs; Neild, Davies Holmes, Barnes, E. Dillon, Eyre, Molyneux, Isherwood, and Beard, forwards. Barrow: Jones, back ; Bowker, Hindle, and Barnett, three-quarters; Waits and Haney, half backs; Cox, Wolveridge, Halsall, Fell, Wilscn, Babbs, Woodend, Sharpe, and J. Bewker, forwards. After the game the visitors were entertained by the Barrow club, ' and a moseenjoyable evening was spent. • I

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 4, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 4, 1890

ever; from some loose play Dillon commenced a move- ment in which he was heartily joined by his cetnrades, and after Hastings had shown rare form, the oval found its way to the hands of Massey.".'who finally man- aged to score near the corner flag. Frank Turner took the place without success. Massey was hurt in respond- ing to the drop-out, and was absent from the game ten minutes. Shaw got away from the line-out, and although Lawless put in a huge kick to Marshall, who failed to respond, the Barrow men, by the aid of Dicken- son and Whitehead. changed the venue to the home quar- ters. Hastings and Fair. Turner failed to utilize a grand chance of scoring,and although Evans' defence was taxed by the vigorous efforts ot the Northerners, the smart Warrington back was equal to any emergency. Barnes tackled Marshall near the line, and eventually a minor fell to Barrow. At half time the score was, Warrington one try; Bairow, one minor. No time was lost in restarting, and some pretty exchanges were the open- ing items of the second half. Barnes here received a grand pass from Bate, but Hartley was down on shim, and danger was averted. Woodburn was at fault imme- diately after, and it was indeed marvellous how the Warringtonians were kept from scoring. This state of things did not last long, for 80111 P loose play of an excit- ing nature was witnessed at he Barrow twenty-five,and a fine effort by Donohue ultimately ended in Frank Turner scoring, the same player kicking a net goal. Whitehead showed up prominently after the restart, and neat exchanges were again loudly applauded. Barnes essayed a drop at goal, the ball striking the posts. Nevins struggled hard from a line-out,and made matters lively for the Barrow backs. The visitors struggled hard to relieve the pressure, but the desired effect was not produced until Dickenson got away, his career being stayed by Thorniley and Donohue. The Warrington custodian again gave the Barrow men a taste of his abilities as a back, and repeatedly cleared his line in a surprising fashion. A long drop at the Barrow citadel went outside the posts, and although the ball was worked to the opposite end, Randles rushed the game to the half way flag, where it finally remained, the whistle bringing an hour's play to a conclusion the final score reading—Warrington, 1-1-1 ; Bariow;o-0-1. The game was exceedingly fast trom start to finish. Evans, although faulty at the commencement, played Williantly- towards the close. Indeed, it is not saying too much that he was far away the best back on the field. Of the other backs the centre three-quarters seemed to have a special mission of watching each other, and the display at this position was far below what sore are accustomed to witnessing. There was ' nothing to choose amongst the other backs, but in the forwards on the home side, Donohue, Nevins, Randles, and Hastings were the pick. In the Barrow ranks Marshall, Dickenson, Whitehead, Shaw, and R. Todd were the best.

_ Teams :—Warrington: J. W. Evans, back; Lawless, T. Barnes, and J. T. Massey, three-quarter backs; W. Antrobus and J. T. Bate, half backs; Fair Turner. Frank Turner, W. Dillon, W. Povey, W. Handles, J. T. Thorniley, W. Nevins, 'P. Donohue, and Hastings, for- wards. Barrow: J. Woodburn. back ; Marshall, J. W. Harley and E. Lockett, three-quarters ; Whitehead and Dickenson, half backs ; A. Harley, Smith. Leake, Simpson, Shaw, Bolton, J. Todd, R. Todd, Corcoran, forwards. Referee, Mr. H. Williamson, Salford Foot- ball Club.
WARRINGTON v. DEWSBURY.

Following their well-earned victory over Barrow ol Saturday, the Warringtonians journeyed te Dewsbury on Wednesday, when the home team were met at Crown Flatts. A large crowd of holiday-geekers welcomed the appearance of the Lancastrians, who unfortunately had to deplore the abseneii of Antrobus, their smart half- back, and Littlewood. Dewsbury, on the other hand, placed a strong fifteen on the field. Warrington were represented by Evans, back ; Massey, Barnes, and P. R Lawless, three-quarters ;J. Bate and J. Lawless, half- backs; W. Dillon, W. Bandies, W. Povey, T. Donohue,. W. Nevins, Frank Turner, Eyres, E. Dillon, and Fair. Turner (captain). Dewsbury: Scott, back; Naylor, Brook, and Grabam, three-quarters; Stadden and For- rest, half backs; Longman, Garforth, Randall, , Morris,. Jackson, Boardman, Gee, Howarth, and Grendhill. Warrington losing the toss, Frank Turner started operations, the oval gravitating in touch near the corner flag. A pass to Graham was mulled, and Warrington rushed the oval in dangerous proximity to the Dewsbury goal. Relief was brought abomt by Stadden, but a fine piece of work by the trio dof Warrington three-quarters found Lawless punting high up to Scott, who mulled, and the Lancashire forwards rushed over the line, but through some alleged informality the point was dis- allowed. Not tb be denied, the visiting for Wards, headed by Dillon and Donohue, again pressed Dewsbury, and only the smart play of Redden and Naylor pre- vented them from accomplishing their desired object. : The tall kicking of the home backs served them to advantage, and negatived many a fine dribble made by Warrington. Grand passing by Eyres Bate, and J. Lawless was neutralized by Longman arid Randall, and then Nevins came in for mtice with a run and kick to 1 the half way flag. The ga7ne still continued of an ex- ' citing and fast nature, and each goal in turn was assailed. An effort by Stadden was frustrated by Evans, and although Nevins was afforded a free kick for a fair catch this did not ease the pressure. The Dewsbury backs indulged in some fine passing, and although' Graham was afforded a fine chance, Massey pounced on him and floored him before he could make headway. Barnes tackled Brooke at the half-way flag, and although Bate struggled to break through the home defence,. the fine play of Stadden and Naylor kept the leather well in the Warrington quarters. Grand exchanges were wit-: nessed between Lawless and Scott, and from a kick by Naylor the ball travelled full forty yards beyond the goal line. Naturally Warrington gave up any idea of racing to kick the ball dead, and Jackson, a Des. sbury forward, stole a march on them and grounded at this distance without any opposition being offered. A point was raised as to the legitiniacy of the try, but Mr. Sewell,the referee, decided in favour of Dewsbury. arguing that no limit had been made regarding the dead ball line. The kick at goal failed. Soon after the drop Out some ex- change kicks ended in favour of Dewsbury, and a minor was recorded from a long punt by Graham. War- rington still defended; the pressure being slightly eased by the aid of some good passing between Lawless and Barnes. A tall kick by Graham again forced a miner, but immediately, on the restart, a grand effort by the .visiting front rank caused Scott some anxiety, and for a time the defence of Dewsbury was severely tested. Stadden again carnet° the rescue of his side, with a fine kick into touch, and his efforts being seconded by similar piece of play on the part of Naylor, the Warring- ton line was again reached. Frank Turner now effected a grand run from a line-out, and a beautifulpass,whieh, if taken, would have resulted in a certain score, was missed, and play was still confined to the Warring- ton twenty-five. Forrest essayed to break away, but found his match in J. Lawless. Subsequently, Forrest passed to Naylor, and the last-named dropped a goal in fine style, this bringing the first half to a close with the score—Dewsbury, one goal, , one try ; War- rington, nil. Warrington had now the advantage of the slight wind, but immediately on the re-start by Brooks looked like ending in disaster -for the visitors. Danger was averted through the effective tackling, and front a pack which followed, Bate and Lawless passed well, finally throwing to Barnes, who ran and kicked into touch beyond the half way flag. Slowly but surely the oval was worked to the Dewsbury end, and although Graham looked like clearing, his progress was checked by Fair Turner. Warrington were now playing in vigorous style, and after the visiting skipper had tried to get away from a line-out, Bandies started a movement which was brilliantly responded to by his comrades.. Donohue took up the swing, and after making a \ gravid ' effort, he was somewhat pressed, but the smart following up of the Lancashire men served them well, for Eyres taking the pass rushed over the line, and an unmistak- able try was scored. Frank Turner failed at the place. With the hope of still gaining the lead, the Warring- tonians played up fearlessly, and the Tykes were again busy with defensive tactics irinnediately on the restart. 'Massey and^ Barnes put in some grand kicks to the Dewsbury line. A fine pass to Massey found him racing across the field and passing to his companion wing three-quarter, Lawless, whose run and kick were brilliantly responded to by Graham. War- rington would not be denied, and Bate throwing to Massey, the last narnal sent the oval :.to Scott, who missed, ind a race for the oval ended in a maul. This resulted in favour of J. Lawless, but Frank Turner upon whom now depended .the isaue, made a grand though unsuccessful bid for goal. Dewsbury now rallied,and by the aid of smart footwork, the homesters were placed on the aggressive. Povey and E. Dillon dribbled accur- ately through the home defence, but a piece of play on the part of Naylor neutralized the effort, and the venue was changed to the Warrington twenty-five. Grand pass- ing by the Warrington backs was loudly applauded,but to no purßose, the covered point was not be got. , Evans made his mark behind the line,and smart following up by Fair Turner sent the ball well into the Dewsbury 25. Near the close Warrington unfortunately lost the services of Barnes, and although P. R. Lawless made a couple of grand efforts to gat in, it was all to no pur- pose, and a grand game was brought to a conclusion ,with the score—Dewsbury, one goal, one try, and ' two minors; Warrington two tries. A better ganhe could scarcely be wished for, but the chief credit for the capital display made by Warrington must be given to .the forwards, who one and all played ,grainily. All through they . displayed a determination that was highly commendable. Of the backs Massey, Evans, Lawless, and Bate 're the pick.

A disastrous explosion of as occurred on Wednesday evening at the residence of Mr. Jones, Ritson- street, Briton Ferry: The interior of the house and contents were greatly damaged, and. aeveral children injured.

div.head: RUNCORN v. LEEDS ST. JOEIN'S.
div.p: RUNCORN v. LEEDS ST. JOEIN'S.

In the presence of about 3,000 spectators these teams met at Runcorn, on Saturday. The weather was fine, though cold, and the ground was well suited to a fast game. The Rune3rn captain won the toss, and Lord kicked off at 3.30, for St. John's. Play at once became fast and exciting. After a few scrimmage Sin Runcorn 25, Faulkner relieved pressure by a dribble, and there was a fair display of punting between Simon and Brazendale. St. John's now pressed, and Burrell put in a dangerous punt near the line, but Brazendale coolly averted danger by making his mark. On the drop out, the Runcorn forwards worked the ball past the half-way flag, where Gayter made a capital dribble, and Hughes saving the return, passed to Crompton, who put in a serviceable run and kick, and Wilkinson was well collared on the line by Faulkner. The home,ters made little use of the opportunity, Wilkinson relieved, and W. Hughes missa ;n the ball, the visitors once more invaded the Runcorn 'territory. The home forwards were, however, not to be denied, and going with a corn-. bined rush, in which Riley was conspicuous, compelled the visitors to touchdown. W. Hughes obtained a free kick in a favourable position. and following up well, the return was Saved. From the scrimmage Abrams dribbled over the line, and P. Riley, being at hand, dropped on the ball and scored the first try amid enthu- siastic cheers. A few minutes later Gayter got hold out of a loose scrimmage, and after the sphere had passed through the hands of W. Hughes, Broady, and Faulkner, P. Riley carried it over the line. Crompton failed at an easy place. After some give-and-take play, Crompton followed up a kick ef Abrams, and scored the third try under the posts, and he safely guided the ball ova the crossbar. A remarkable piece of play was now shown by Brazendale, who rushed through the Leeds pack, and badly finished up a brilliant run by passing forward. Strive as they would, the visitors could not make any headway, the locals working with admirable spirit and combination. A brilliant exchange between Davies and Crompton resulted in the fatter player eluding his opponents,a.nd grounding behind the posts kicked a goal. Half-time was called with the game standing Runeorn, 3 goals 1 try 1 miner t. John's, nil. On resuming play immediately settled in the visitors' quarters, and a series of scrimmages having taken place,Crompton made a run to the line and when on the point of being tackled passed to Davies, who scored near the corner flag. Brazen- dale failed to convert. Again the attack was resumed, the pace apparently being much too fast for the Leeds men wlso struggled hopelessly On, and Evans catching the ball from a line out, rushed under the posts, and Crompton kicked his third goal. A relief to the mono- tony, came in a rush by the,Leeds forwards who reached , the home line, but their stay was brief, Faulkner, Broady, Hancock and P. Riley coming away with the ball at their feet. A period of fine dribbling passing and running occurred with no result, but in a few minutes of time, Evans threw to Crompton who treated the spectators to a splendid dodgy run, and ended pass- ing to Davies who darted round the opposing side, and planted the ball under the posts. Crompton failed in his ' attempt at goal. Gayter was next conspicuous with a ' long run, but a wild pass, nullified any advantage that might have occurred, and the final result was Runcorn, 4 goals 3 tries 1 minor; Leeds St. John's, nil. Teams: —Leeds St. John's : F. F. Wilkinson, pack; P. Bate, 'l'. Simon, and D'Arcy Thompson, three-quaiters : T. Smith and B. Burrell, half backs ; E. G. Load, H. M. Hepper, ; J. Wood, H. Davies, Lister, Stone, J. Watmough, W. Cope, ' and C. Hirst. Runcorn: Bratendale, back; Davies, Crompton, H. Hughes, three-quarters ; Evans, and Abrams, half hacks ; Broady. W. Hughes, Gayter, P. Riley, Hancock, Dolon, Faulkner, Rigby, and Hamp- son. Referee : Mr. R. Wilcock. • WARRINGTON v. BARROW-IN-FURNESS.

This fi'xture, one of the most interesting on the War- rington card, was played on the ground of the iirst- named club on Saturday, in the presence of some 3,000 spectators. The Barrow men had whipped together their strongest team, and when it is taken into account that their latest achievement had resulted in Broughton Rangers being beaten by three goals to one, it looked on paper that Warrington would have all their work cut out to win. Previous matches have always with one exception resulted in decisive wins for Warrington, and the games have been of so interesting a description that the visit of the Barrovians is awaited with plea- sure.

The ground was in grand condition,. and Harley, the latest recipient of county honours and captain of the visiting team, started towards the pavilion goal. The Barrow men having a look in, their forwards rushed down the fieldat a terrific speed,their stay being effected through the smartness of Evans. Lawless next put in a fine kick, and his speed served him to advantage, for followiag up his kick he tackledLockett with the oval in his possession, and again the Barrow goal was in jeopardy. Some wild passing by the home backs gave Lockett a chance, but he was pulled up at the home quarter flag, and although the Furness men attacked for a lengthened period, it was of no avail, they could not ,cross the line: Lawless was to the fore with a smart kick, and Donohue and Fair Turner were useful in a line- out. Despite the fact that Antrobus was slightly hurt, and had to temporarily retire, the home forwards, headed by Povey, Dillion' and Bandies, ryished the leather to within a yard ot the Barrow line.' Marshall punted well to Evans, and Barrow were afforded a line chance of scoring, bin in their eagerness to notch a tan- gible score they infringed the offside rule, and were ac- cordingly penalized. By this aid Warrington relieved, , and the next item worthy of notice was Bate struggling through the pack, the safe tackling of Whitehead alone preventing him from accomplishing his object. How-

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

To-day's matches :—Warrington V. Tyldesley (league match) at Warrington; Runcorn v. Wakefield Trinity at Wakefieid ; Widnes v, Ratcliffe at Ratcliffe; St. Helens v. Rochdale St. Clements at St. Helens; St. Helens Recs. v. Aspull at Aspull.

The match with Barrow is a rather popular one in Warrington, and it generally leads to a display of some good football. The name of Saturday, though Warring- ton had a good pull in points at the end, was a fairly even one. The Barrovians are strong in scrimmaging and fine dribblers, and they often severely tested the defensive qualities of the home backs. On the whole, however, the play was not up to the highest standard, of either club, as it was sometimes of a scrambling nature, and there was not much of the combined passing one sometimes sees.

The meeting to-day of Tyldesley and Warrington on the ground of the latter, is an interesting event, and it will be all the more interesting because it is a League match. In their fit* encounter of the season, two or three weeks ago, ryldesley came off victors on their own ground, and it is certain that the " wirepullers" will try their best to equalise matters. The Warringtonians have not been very successful in the League fixtures so far. Will they do better this time?

There is something singularly consistent about the play of the Warrington "A " team. No matter where or when or whom they play they always seem able to "rub it in "in the most satisfactory style. When the scores come to be compiled at the end ot the season they must have a tremendous balance of goals and tries—especially tries, for goal-kicking seems to be the only weak point about the team—over their opponents.

The St. Helens Recs. accomplished one of their best performances, and one which gave the greatest satisfac- tion to their supporters, last Saturday. This was the administration of a decisive defeat on their old rivals Wigan. By this time everybody in St. Helens knows how the Recs. piled on the agony and how, after half-time, Wigan were never in it. The feat of the Recs. is rendered all the more praiseworthy by the fact that the battle was fought on the Wigan ground, and the supporter's of the home contingent might well cry after the match "Oh, what a surprise."

The Hunslet (Leeds) team had the St. Helens (town) club as visitors last Saturday, and they entertained their friends from Lancashire to the tune of a four goals and one try defeat. St. Helens wore,, as usual, weakhanded and from the commencement the glassblowers had no chance with their redoubtable opponents.

The record of matches played by the St. Helens Rem up to Saturday last, shows 12 won, four lost, and one drawn, out of a total of 17 played; while the St. Helens Club record is as under : 20 played, seven won, twelve lost, and one drawn. Whilst the Rees have scored 19 goals, 3$ tries, and 54 minors, to 8-15-42 by their oppon- ents, the St. Helens team have obtained 11 goals, 25 tries and 54 minors to 15 goals, 18 tries and .45 minors against them.

Runcorn were in great form after their return from South Wales, where they met the first defeat of the season. On Boxing day they defeated Birmingham Old Edwardians by five goals one try to nil, and on Saturday Leeds St. John's retired beaten to the extent of four goals three tries to nil. The last result was the most surprising,as the Leeds club has been lately showing fine form. The dry ground exactly suited the Runcorn team, who set so fast a pace that Leeds were never in it after the first ten minutes. The home team islayed well to a man and it would be invidious to particularise.. After the match the teams sat down to dinner at the Cafe, Mr. and Mrs. Riley catering in their customary admirable manner.
FIRST WARRINGTON STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.

The third annual meeting of the 826th Starr- Bowkett Building Society, was tleld in Legh-st. Schoolroom, on Thursday evening, and the pro- ceedings were presided over by Mr. „John Walker, the chairman of the Society. In opening the meet- ing the chairman said they had every reason to be gratified at the progress which Starr-Bowkett Building Societies hail made in Warrington. Two societies, had completed their full number of members and the third society was being organised and would commence to receive payments on Saturday evening. The past year had,commerciallyspeaking,been a fairly prosperous one, and there was every reason to believe that the year upon which they had just entered would be equally prosperous. He trusted that the members of that Society, and the working classes generally, would make the best use of their earnings, and in these better times put something carefully aside for less prosperous days. They would see from the report that their own society continued to make progress, the balance of profit up to the present time being £7O Gs. sd. (Applause.) The minutes of the previous meeting were then read and adopted.

div.head: DLRECTORS' REPORT AND THE BALANCE SHEET.
div.p: THE DLRECTORS' REPORT AND THE BALANCE SHEET.

The Directors' annual report was then read. It stated that "the total income for the year ending November Ist, 1889, from all sources, amounts to £1,850 us. 10d., the balance of profit being £7O 6s. sd. During the year six appropriations have been made, amounting to £1,500. The total number ballotted since the commencement of the Society is 16, amounting to £4,600. Of these eleven have been advanced £3,500 ; one appropriated is now ready at the bankers, and the other accumulating. The following directors retire, and, being eligible, offer them- selves for re-election :—Messrs. George Lea, William I Cranipton, John Griffiths, and David Sumner. The auditors, Messrs. William Milliard and Frederick Pear- son also retire, and, being eligible, offer themselves for re-election." Mr. Titchett, one of the secretaries, next read the balance sheet,. whith was unanimously adopted after it had been stated, in answer to a question, that a depreciation of 20 per cent, upon the books was ample for the purpose.

div.head: _ ELECTION OP DTRECTONS, &C. -• • –
div.p: _ ELECTION OP DTRECTONS, &C. -• • -

As stated in the directors' report, the retiring direc- tors were Messrs. G. Lea, W. Crampton, J. Griffiths, and D. Sumner. A letter was read from Mr. Griffiths, stating that he was unable to attend the meeting, and that he was not desirous of again being appointed a director. To All the vacancies, tll4- following gentlemen were nominated :—Messrs. W. Hickman' J.Colledge, .7. G. Brown,. D. Sumner, J. Whittle, G. Lea, and W. Crampton. On a ballot beine. taken the voting resulted as follows :—Mr. Drown, 27 Mr. Hickman, 16;' Mr. Sumner, 15 ; Mr. Crampton, 15; Mr. Celled:re, 13; Mr. ; Lea, 11 ; Mr. Whittle, 9. The four first-named were, I consequently,. declared elected. Mr. WI Mull:ad and Mr. I F. Pearson were re-elected auditors.

div.head: TE muxor.
div.p: TE muxor.

Mr. Hickman was -elected io Preside over the ballot for the seventeenth appropriation. Mr. J. Andrews and Mr. G. J. Brown were elected scrutineers, and the ballot balls were drawn by John Cox. The ballot resulted in the number 203 being drawn, this number entitling Mr. Hugh Fairhurst Greenough, of Horsemarket-st., to the use of £4OO, free of interest for 121- years. The meeting was brought to a close with votes of thanks to the chairman, scrutineers, &c.

FUNERAL OF DR. MACKAY. The remains of the late Dr. Mackay, author of "sheer boys, cheer," and other songs, were on Thursday con- veyed from Earl's Court, Loadon, where he died on Tuesday week, to the Kemal Green Cemetery, where the funeral took place, in the presence of numerous friends and relatives.

TREAT TO THE AGED AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday the custom was again observed of giving to the aged poor of Warrington a treat in the way of a substantial meal, that was served in the Public Hall, many, willing helpers giving askistance in attending to the wants of the guests. As usual, the old men had dinner at noon, and the aged women had tea at six o'clock, followed by a very enjoyable entertainment At noon the guests numbered about 400, and they made havoc of a good old fashioned English dinner, the viands disappearing - with surprising rapidity. The Committee by whom the arrangements had been made consisted of Alderman Sutton (president), Mr. Thos. Jones (vice-president), Alderman Wright (secre- tary), Mr. Thos. Morris (hon. treasurer), Messrs. P. Cal-dwell, P. Chrimes, W. H. Robinson Chas. Skinner, Jas. Smethurst, Daniel Jones, D. Fanslaw, G. Pilling, Samuel Jones. Amongst those present, most of whom helped to wait on the guests, and some of whom made themselves specially useful, were the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Francomb,) the Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis), Mrs. Willis, Alderman Sutton, Alderinan Wright, Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, G. Allton, S. ffilkinson, E. H. Jackson, and F. Timins, Dr. Peacocke, Messrs. T. Morris, John Harrison, S. Jones, R. T. Smith, J. Smethurst, P. Chrimes, G. Pilling, Wm. Sharp, C. Skinner. D. Fanshaw, H. Toft, G. Riley, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs, Venn, Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Chrimes, and many others. During the progress of the meal Mr. W. S. Woods played selections on the organ. When the appetites of all the old men had been appeased, tobacco and pipes were distributed, and speechmaking followed.—Alder- man Surrox said that as preparations had to be made for the tea for the old ladies, there was not much time for speech-making, but there was one thing that they always did at those gatherings, and that was to drink the health of her Majesty the Queen. When the Queen ascended the throne many of the old men present were children, and as he did not think any of them would like to part with her Majesty, he was sure that they would all wish that she might enjoy many happy years to come. The guests then cheered for the Queen, and the toast was accorded musical honours. Cheers were also given for the Prince of Wales, after which Mr. Sutton, who is president of the association, said that since they last met to partake of the annual dinner, many changes .had taken place, and many friends had departed this life. He did not think that any of those present would fail to miss the genial faces of two , good old friends who had been in the habit of attending those gatherings for many years past. It would be pain- fully manifest to them that that there were two good old friends missing this year—the late Alderman John Pier- point and the late Mr. J. W. Horton. Mr. Pierpoint had been connected with the Institution for more than a quarter of a century; in fact from the commencement of it. During the latter part of that time he occupied the position of president of the Association. He did not think any one ever took such a deep interest in the matter as did the late Mr. Pierpoint. Their other friend, Mr. Horton, was never so happy as when he was attend- ing to the welfare and happiness of all the old people and the poor of the town. He was very pleased indeed to see that the guests were all looking so well as they did. He never saw them look better, and he hoped that they would all have a prosperous Year. (Applause.) —The Rector, who was called upon for a speech, said that it had been a very great pleasure to him tobe present, and to be allowed the privilege of contributing towards the dinner. We had it on high authority that it was more blessed to give than to receive. That was, he thought, one of those occasions on which it came home to one that it was a great privi- lege and happiness to be able to do something towards] the aged, and for their friends. Such an occasion brought home to them the fact that they were brothers and that they should take the deepest interest in each others welfare. He hoped that the year just com- menced would to them be a happy one.—. The Rev. S. • Wilkinson remarked that they were all pleased to see the Rector present. Although he had not been long in Warrington .he had endeared himself to their hearts by his zealous work in the cause of God. He wished those present a prosperous year in the highest sense of the word. Dur- ing the last twelve months they had lost some of their most distinguished townsmen. He thought that they had lost something like eight or ten men who had for many years past worked for the -good of Warrington in a . great number of ways. On an occasion like that their thoughts must go back to Mr. John Pierpoint, who for so many years was president of the association, and Mr. Hcrton who was such a melons worker in the cause. In conclusion, he thought that one of the best wishes he could give them was—" may 'good digestion wait on • appetite."—The proceedings were then brought to a con- clusion.

About 450 aged women had tea in the evening, the ladies and gentlemen who looked after their wants being the same who gave their services at the dinner, with a few additions. 4 tremendous quantity of beef and ham had been cut up, sandwiches forming a very important part of the feast, to which the old ladies devoted t them- selves with much assiduity. After tea, through the kindness of an anonymous donor, each guest received a. present of a quarter of a pound of tea and a pound of sugar. Soon after six o'clock the general public were admitted to the gallery, which was crowded long before ' the time announced for the commencement of the con- cert. As soon as the tea and sugar had been handed round, and quiet restored, Alderman Sutton addressing those present, again referred to the deaths of Alderman Pierpoint, and Mr. W. J. Horton, and proceeded, to state that last year the receipts of the Committee amounted to £B6 3s. 3d., whilst the expenditure was : £BB. ss. The cost of providing the treat was increasing year by year as the number who wished to avail them- selves of it was always increasing. At the request of Mr. Sutton, the Rector also spoke. He was glad to be. present that evening, for that seemed one of those very. happy occasions on which the donors of the feast felt' that they were conferring no favour, and the recipients 9 felt that they were receiving none.—The Rev. S. Wilkin-- son proposed a resolution according the thanks of those. present to. Alderman Sutton. the president, Alderman. Wright, the secretory, and Mr. T. Morris, the treasurer%, for their services.—The proposition having been carried with applause, Alderman Sutton, in reply, said that tile Committee did their very best to promote the success.of the Association.—Mr. Morris, who also replied, appealed for additional aid. He had-only got about £2O in hand towards the next treat, and it should be about £7.80: Alderman Wright, in acknowledging the resolution of thanks, referred to the readiness with which the tor,ens- people responded. to the appeal of the Committee for fonds, and to the pleasure that it seemed to afford them‘to,con- tribute to such a worthy object.--Subsequently so ngs,were rendered by Mrs. Sutton. Miss Faoshow, Mr.. Fansliaw, Mr. 'kin, Mr. W. Bellian, and Mr. G. Baxter, .atnitecita- tions were given by Mr. Furness. During the ewening Mr. Brinstey Sheridan, from the Theatre lim.xtl;, with several members of his Company, gave the trial' scene from " Greltey's Money," Mr. Sheridan appearing as "Soft Tommy Shuttleworth," a character that hoe been represented by him over 2;299 times. It should be mentioned that the vocalists were accompanied) on the piano by Mr. Geo. Riley, and that Mr. W, S. 'nods was at the organ.

, ASSAULT ON A GIRL.--OR SatMrday, at ho Newton 1 Petty Sessions, Michael Owen, who was c.onvicted a few weeks ago on a,charge o 5 a.ssanking to little girls near ' Warrington, was again ehargvd with having as,saulted a tittle girl named Emmeline ving, who, lives at Crow, 'lane, Newton. The complainant said that on the 22nd May last the,defendant accosted her in Grange-road, and asked if she-had been to school. She replied that she had not, whereupon the defendant said "I will make you go," and knocked her.down, kicked her several times, and three her over the hedge. She screamed, and the defendutr ran oft In the, direction,of Ilaydock. was given by Minas Leigh anciLydia Martha Lewis.. At two o'clock on Sunday morning a collision occurred at Tower Point, a f ,w miles fronvGreenock, between the ,to-amship Ovington, of Maryport, bound from Glasgow tor Hamburg, with coals, and the Bteamship Queen Victoria. The former vessel was cut down below the water-line, and settled down directly after the collision. The steward, three firemen, and a boy were carried 4°n with the Ovington, and were all drowned, the remainder being saved. The Queen Victoria is believed to have proceeded, her injuries not being great.

SHOCKING CRUELTY TO CHILDREN. Two MOTHEES COMMITTED TO PRISON. • On Monday at the Town Hall, before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. A. Walmesley-Cothatn, Elizabeth Brown, alias Smith, of Sandfield Crescent, was charrd under the Prevention of Cruelty to •Chil- dren a Act, with illtreating and neglecting her infant ' daughter, aged 12 months, thereby causing injury to the health of the child. Chief Constable Wood stated that the prisoner and a man named Smith came into the town and lodged in Sandfield Crescent. Since then she had been often seen to strike the child with her fist and open hand, and had been seen to ' kick it off a stool. She had not supplied it with proper food, and had left the child all day in the house. A Mrs. Kennedy had asked the prisoner to take the child to the hospital, but she said it could die before she took it there. For the past five weeks it had been the cus- tom of the prisoner to strike the child, to kick it, to keep it without clothing, and she had often expressed a wish that it would die. On Saturday afternoonlast, a police- , man was called in and the prisoner then seized the child by the legs, and threatened to knock its brains out against the wall. The officer took the woman into cus- tody, and the child was carried to Dr. MeNicoll, who found it to be suffering from starvation. It was really nothing but skin and bone.—Evidence was then given by Mary Ann Kennedy, wife ot Thomas Kennedy, of 28, Sandfield, Crescent, who said she had seen the prisoner strike the baby with her clenched fist, and kick it from a stool. A week ago her (witness's) husband struck the prisoner because of her ill-treatment of the child.—Mrs. Bradley, lodging- house keeper, Mrs. Smith, a neighbour, Dr. McNicoll, and P.C. Winnard gave corroborative testimony.—The prisoner said she had never kicked the child in her life. She said she had given it all the food she possibly could, and was, herself, often without food for a whole day.— The Chairman: That is no excuse for beating and ill- treating the child.—Chief Constable Wood said the woman had an immoral character.—The prisoner: I was obliged to do something when he left me to the mercy of the world.—The Bench committed her to pri- son for two months. At the Police Court, on Tuesday, before Alderman J. Meßryde and M:. B. Biram, Mary Creegan, a young married woman, of Liverpool-road, was charged with being drunk, and causing her son Michael, four years old, to be in the street for the purpose of begging. Police-constable Sellers stated that about six o'clock on Monday night he saw prisoner in Talbot-st. She was carrying a child eightben months old, and the boy Michael was by her side. She was in a drunken condi- tion, and after attempting to sing, she sent the little fellow, who was shivering with cold, to beg. Witness had previously cautioned her for the same offenee.—Sergeant Hunter said the prisoner was the wife of a sober, steady man, who gave her 21a week to keep house on. He gave her 18s. en Friday last, and on Saturday she was found helplessly drunk. On Mondaynight her husband was at work, and there was not a bit of supper for him. Prisoner went out begging, and spent the money in drink.—Prisoner said she was very sorry, and if they would let her go this time she would not offend again. Her family had lived in St. Helens one hundred years, and she was the first to get into trouble. Her father had worked for Colonel Gamble for thirty-five years.—The Husband : I give her money regularly, and she should not go on like this. —Chief Constable Wood said prisoner had been twice

About nine years ago, the Runcorn Board oi Guardians achieved a notoriety which furnished jests for pantomime humourists, and the .present dilemma over the appointment of a schoolmaster may result in a similar unenviable distinction. In October the schoolmaster, Mr. Stubbing. 'resigned his position on the advice of the Goyernment Inspector, and the Board accepted his resignation at once, because it was evident there was a game of cross purposes on-foot which was•not to the advan- tage of the Union. Through the influence of his friends on the Board, Mr. Stubbing was permitted to apply for the post he had vacated, and a fort- night ago he was re-appointed instructor Zo the rising youths of the Workhouse by a large majority. The Local Government Board refuse to stamp the appointment with their official approval, in conse- quence of certain circumstances within their know- ledge, and on Tuesday the Guardians, by a narrow majority, decided not to ask the London Board for a more full and explicit explanation. The situation as it stands at present is a very pretty: one. Two members have given notice of their intention toimov e the selection of tvvo'3liffe- rent candidates as schoolmaster, and Mr. Jeffs has notified that he will propose that Mr. Stub- bing shall be allowedto fulfil those duties to which a majority of the representatives of the Union have appointed him in spite of !`lly lords." Usually the work of the Union is carried', on by about a dozen of the 42 elected Guardians: but there will be 'a rare xi:Meter at the next Meeting of the Board, wben the aid of the ,Government Inspector will be invoked"to cut the gordian knot. But will there be wisdom amongst the "multitude of counsellors"? The house dinner of the RiincOrn Liberal Clun, on Monday, was not a pretentious affair by any means, but it brought together a considerable number of the party for a few hours' social enjoyment. and this served a very good purpose. Several capital speeches were delivered, and those present had the pleasure of hearing narrated interesting personal reminiscences of the speakers. • Mr. Wynne Humphreys touched upon a matter well worthy the attention of Liberals. It is fashion- able to decry the introduction of politics 'into local affairs, but the State is governed by political partis- ans, to the general advantage, and what is good for the country at large ought surely to be good for a municipality. The minds of the Runcorn Commissioners have been greatly exercised of late on the great question of" Flags y. tiles," and on Thursday they decided that property owners must pave the parapets in front ,of their properties with flags, before the Com- missioners will undertake the responsibility of keeping the streets in repair. If it be good that the property owners should use flags, it should not need any argument to show that it is good for the Board to flag the unpaved por- tions of the streets under their control, and replace with flags the tiles already set, as they are worn out. This is demanded in common fairness to all concerned.

THE MUSEUM RATING.

Sir,—l beg to apologise. I was not aware that the " Examiner " had "demonstrated" that a pennYin the pound would free the Library, and Id. leave a surplus of over £lOO for the better maintenance of the Library, Museum, and Art Gallery. I say I did not know this. , But it appears to have been examined and found correct by the "Examiner ;" but has the Museum Committee, who are responsible for the management of the concern written Q. E. D. beneath the "Examiner's" solution of this problem ? Now, sir, while conceding to every one the full right and liberty to differ from me in matters of opinion, I must strongly protest against a wilful perversion of fact. The recommendation by the Museum Committee that the limit be 2d. in the pound, was passed without a single dissentient vote. Hence am I not warranted in saying the Committee were unanimous in their recom- mendation? And this notwithstanding the versatility of that unique member who had the felicity to agree with you in this matter, but was silent at the meeting of the Committee and adverse at the Council. So I repeat the Museum Committee unanimously recommended 2d. as the limit of the rate.—l am, &c., JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 30th Dec., 1889.

We do not care to split hairs with our correspondent; it comes to this, that .the Library Committee were "un- animous "—that is, of one mind, but there was one member of the Committee who was so much of another mind that he spoke and voted in the Town Council against the proposal to raise the rate to more than 10. Mr. reers seems to think the Library Com- mittee everything—since he became a member of it ; we don't. It is, or should be. the servant, not the master of the ratepayers ; and it is for the ratepayers to say whether the advance shall be one of a id. or a id. in the pound. And why does our correspondent charge us with "a wilful perversion of fact?" This means that we have lied—not simply made a mis- statement. Has he forgotten that, quite recently, he said he should knock the man down who charged him with lying? And is he such a "chartered libertine" as to think the charge is to be tolerated when he makes it? That Mr. Peers may see that we have no desire to avoid "fair and free discussion," we call upon him to make good his accusation—or to again apologise.—En.

div.head: "THE BLACK SPOTS OF WARRINGTON."
div.p: "THE BLACK SPOTS OF WARRINGTON."

- -------- Sir,—l am glad you have called public attention to the very unsanitary condition of miny places in "the good old town of Warrington." But I am somewhat 89rry that you have not persisted in your enterprise, and gone more into detail. Perhaps, however, you think it shonld now be a question for the ratepayers to take up, and especially for such as earnestly desire to see prnressmade in sanitary reform. Ido not intend in this letter to do more than say that the Sanitary Committee of the Town Council will be wise to leave off their debates and quarrels about the Longford DepOt, and turn their attention to necessary work in various parts of this town. I am hoping that public opinion in this community will soon be thoroughly aroused as to the urgent importance of all kinds of sam- tary reform. It is only the force of outside opinion that will really influence our municipal legislators. I trust that next November any municipal elections that may occur will not be fought upon political grounds, which are worse than stupid in such a matter, but upon the questions of personal fitness, and municipal policy. This town needs many things to be done which the public will have themselves in this way to initiate. We must send men to the Council who will go in for clean dwell- ings, sound drainage, and proper roads. And , also men who will not hesitate to condemn propertewhich is not fit for animals, much less human beings, to live in, no matter who may be its owner. I have asked occasionally of various friends how it is that our authorities are so comparatively supine upon these domestic reforms, and have more than once heard it said, "before they could mend matters generally, some of the would have to mend their own." Surely that is not:the case ! If it is, all the more reason why the public should interfere. Warrington property owners, whoever they may, be, should be made to face their responsibilities, and put their houses in order. I don't envy the man who can take a rent from a dwelling which he kriows is in an unhealthy condition. Such a man is responsible 'for the physical health of his tenant, and he has no right to get a profit at risk of his poorer brother's suffering. Go on, sir, by all means to stir us up to the much needed enterprise of sanitary reform. Having begun, do not cease, one way or another, until our local parlia- ments has no time for its miserable personal quibbling and quarrellings, and has to give its attention to the needs of the people in whose service it is constituted. —Yours faithfully,
JOHN YONGE. 13, Wilson Patten-st., January 1, 1890.

- --- DIVIDEND SOCIETY.—The annual audit of this society took place on Monday evening, atthe Bull's Head Hotel, Lymm, the auditors being Bros. J. Holt (Lymm), and E. Hewitt (High Leigh). The books and vouchers showed that the dividend will be about double the amount dis- tributed last year. • ANNUAL BALL.—The fifth annual ball was held at the Golden Fleece Hotel on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance, dancing commencing at eight o'clock. An extension of time was granted for the occasion, and refreshments were supplied by the landlord, Mr. Lake. TEMPERANCE MEETING.---There was a good attendance at the weekly meeting of the Wesleyan Band of Hope, which was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thorp, and an address was delivered by Mr. T. Moston. In addition to the usual items by: the members, M.. Taylor gave a reading and Miss Marion Thorp sang a solo. Ditittnn OF RAILWAY SERVANTS.—The annual dinner of the railway servants of the North-Western Company at Lymm took place on Thursday night at the residence of Mr. Thomas Jones, the stationmaster at Lymm Station. Seventeen sat`dolwn to an excellent spread provided hy Mrs. Jones, who occupied the ckair. Th company amused themselves during the evening withe songs and games of various descriptions. BAPTIST TEA MEETING.—The annual social tea meeting of the members of the Higher-lane Baptist Chapel took Place on Wednesday evening. After tea the meeting adjourned to the chapel. Mr. James Daviel, C.C. for Bowdon, occupied the chair, and he was strpported by Messrs. Tower and Evans, froyn the Baptist College, Manchester, also Messrs. Diamond, Knowles, Ike. Ad- dresses were given by the Chairman and Messrs. Knotvles, Diamond, Clarke, 13rundrit, Hurstfield, Towers, and Evans. "SHEPHERDS BY NIGHT" LODGF.—The annual audit of the above lodge was held last evening, week, at the Lodge-room, Nag's Head Hotel, Lymm, the auditors being Bro. J. Astley, of Lymm, and Bro. Geo. Astall, of Thelwall. Bro. G. H. Leigh, the secretary, reported that the year had been a most satisfactory one, not only with regard to the increase in new members, but also on account of the amount the lodge had been able to invest during the year. They had at the present time four times the amount invested that they had ten ygars ago, and he hoped this prosperity would continue in the

future. LOCAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the Lymm Local Board took place on Thursday night. There were present Mr. H. Cameron (chairrrtan), Messrs. Dutton, Brazendale, Forster, Gibbon, and Thomason, Mr. Ridg- way (law clerk), Mr. Mullard (clerk), -and Mr. Mint (surveyor) —'-The Law Clerk read a report of the deputa- tion appointed at the last Board meeting to meet the directors of the Water Company. From this it appeared the deputation met the company on Dec. Nth, and after full discussion of the question of carrying the water to Heatley the company declared their inability to do so at the present time, and that they had no desire to press for their legal rights to a guarantee for interest on their out- lay. They were willing to carry the mains to Heatley at the earliest opportunity, and they expected the Board to put in force their powers to compel those who had no proper supply to take water from the mains, but it would probably be a year before they would be in a position to carry out the undertaking.—The report was adopted.—The rest of the business was formal.

RLINCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. .J. W. Lightburn presided, and there were present Messrs. Speakman, Fisher, White, Whittaker, Smith, Imison, Taylor, Hankin- son, Grice, F. A. Lake. (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical, officer), and M. Barker (surveyor). -

COMPLIMENTS OPTHE SEASON. The Chairman having wished all the members a pros- perous New Year, said he was sorry to hear of the death of the wife of one of the metnbers—Mrs. Wass. He was sure they all deeply sympathised with Mr. Wass in his trouble. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Speakman, on behalf of thd Board, reciprocated the good wishes of the Chairman. HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medical Officer reported that the number of dm.ths registered during the past month amounted to 34. This showed an average death-rate for the 12 months of a fraction over 22 per 1,000 of the estimated popblation.

BRICKS V. FLAGS. The Highway and Buildings Committee recommended : That the footway in Greenway-road opposite Mr. Abel's and Mr. J. Kirkham's property be paved with bricks. That all streets before being adopted by the Board in future should have the footpaths flagged, and the streets otherwise made in accordance with the specifications of , the Board. That the plans of Mr: Wm. Leece, for the erection of eight cottages in Albert-st., be adopted.—Mr. Taylor moved the adoption of the minutes with the exception of that referring to Greenveay-road, in order that a full :Board might deal with it.—Mr. Speakman said lie had carefully gone into the question,and he thought it would be a false step for the Board to pave any portion of Greenway-road with bricks, that ought th be paved with flags.—Mr.Fisher said they were compelling property oWtiers to flag parapets, and he did not see why Green- way-road should he an exception.—Mr. Hankinson said there were Several streets already paved with bricks, and ifl,he property owners had to lake up - these and put down flags, he considered it would he an injustice. Mr. Smith moved that the portion of Greenway-road referred tO in the minutes be flagged.—Mr. Once said he would second that motions—The Chairman thought, in view of the absent „members, it would be fair to defer a decision on the matter, and Mr. Taylor's motion was carried with- out dissent,. • THE T.IBRARY COMMITTEE AND CHRISTMAS DAY. The Library Committee submitted the following minutes :—Recommended that 60, volumes be sent to the binder's for rebinding, that the Reading Room be opened on Christmas day, and that the caretaker be allowed ss. for the extra services. which -the change would entail. M. • Harikinson- Moved,' and Mr. Grim e seconded; tile adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Speakman: I think it was a great mistake to open on Christmas Day.—Mr. Giice : Why ?—Mr. Speakman : *Everybody has a ' holi- dAy ; let the caretaker have one. ;The Chairman put the motion to the meeting, and declared it carried.—Mr, Speakman: Christmas Day is over; I presume it meanS next Christmas - day.—Mr, Taylor : The minutes-,a,re,. passed; is this in order.,—The,Chairman : It is not in order.—Mr. Fisher: But you did not ask whether there was any objection to the minittes before you Put them—Mr. Imison : Quite right.—The Chairmen : If you have no objection Mr. Speakman can proceed.— Mr. Speakman thereupon moved an amendment that the news room 'he not opened on Christmas Day.—Mr. Once : Are von referring to next Christmas Day or this Christmas Day.—Mr. Speakman : I am referring to every Christmas Day. If we pass this minute! it means any Christmas Day until it is rescinded.—Mr. Once Do you move that the allowance he not male—Mr. Speak- man: Yes.—The Chairman pointed out that the caretaker had already rendered the services.—Eventually 1889 was added after Christmas Day, and the minute pissed—Mr. Crrice said now the matter was settled, he might, mention that the gentlernars who made the proposition said if the Board would not pay the ss. he would pay it himself. AN APPEAL FROM PROPERTY OWNERS. Mr. Whittaker moved that resolution No. 1285, "That: notices he served on the respective owners of premises fronting, adjoining. or abutting. on Norfolk-sti, to sewer, metal, Sm.:such street. in pursuance of Section 150 of the Public Health Act, 1875." lse rescinded. TIP said the property owners aS well as the Bridgewater Trustees had taken the whole street in hand, and it would he put in order to the satisfaction of all the ratepayers in the street. Mr. Taylor said the street would before . very long have to be made and put in such a condi- tion that the town would adopt it. Ho should, there- fore, he sorry if the owners spent now. ,a fourth of 'the ultimate cost in puttina the street into what they ' called fair order.—Mr. Smith seconded Mr. 'Whittaker's. motion, and elicited that the street was already sewered.—The Chairman read a memorial. sinned by the whole of .the property owners in the street. asking that- the resolution should be allowe'd to remain in abeyance. —Mr. Speakman contended that it would not he fair to other property owners to rescind this resolution, and he said if those interested in this instanee studied their own interest they would not ask for it tobe rescinded.—After further discussion. the Motion was put to the meeting and four voted for it.—Mr. Lake said it was therefore ;ost, as it required two-thirds of those present to rescind a. resolution. It was irrmally understood that Mr. Barker should refrain fr serving the notices at pre- sent. so that Mr. Whittaker might have an opportunity of twinging the question before a larger meeting. SEWER.AGE AND ITIF. SHIP CANAL. • The Chairman said the Ship canal Company had submitted a scheme for sewering Runcorn. The Ilearrl had appointed Mr. Newton, CE. ,of Marmhester,to exam- ine the plans in their interest. He had done so, and had given a report a copy of whichniad been sent to the Ship Canal Company. Mr. Leader Williams.nov: wished for an interview with Mr. Newton on the subject, and it would be necessary for the Commissioners to empower Mr. Newton to hold that interview. After a dismis- sion, which it was thought advisable in the public inter- est should not be published, it was resolved that Mr. Newton should hold the proposed interview.
RITNCAIRN FERRY. The Ship Canal Comoany sent a plan of how they nronosed dealing vrith the Ferry across the Mersey. The snhjoct was referred to the Highway and Buildings Committee.

The St. Helens Recreation and Wakefield Trinity teams met on the Recs. ground, on Wednesday afternoon: The first half was in favour of the Recs., Gerrard scoring a good try. In the second half Pyke gained a second try, Ellison just failing at the place. Final result : Recreation, 2 tries 1 minor ; Wakefield Trinity, 1 minor.

SCALDING FATALITY IN HOYLE-ST. Mr. Samuel Brighouse, Coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an inquiry, on Monde:, afternoon, at the Three Pigeons Inn, Tanner's-lane, regarding the death of a little boy named V, arnest Goskar, six years of age, son of a fish-dealer, who lives in hoyle-st. At about five o'clock on the afternoon of the 21st ult., Pre.ierick Goskar, the father of the deceased, was sitting in the kitchen, and deceased and his sister were playing together. Unfortunately deceased tripped against the hearth-rug, and in falling be caught hold of the handle of a pan con- taining hot water, which was on the fire. This he pulled over, the result being that he was severely scalded about the face, arms, and neck. The father applied oil to the injured parts, and sent for a doctor, but the child succumbed to its injuries yesterday week. The jury found that the death was caused by accident.

OUTIMBAE OF FIRE AT HOWLEY MILLS. At half-past eight o'clock on Tuesday morning, a fire was discovered to have broken out at the Florence Mills, Howley, owned by Mr. H. E. Lees. An alarm was raised, and in a short time the Fire Brigaded under the superintendence of Mr. Turner, together with the fire engine, were at the scene of the conflagration. The fire originated in the dry- iii which adjoins the boiler-house, and it is surmized thatothe heat from this place ignited the goods in the next compartment. The flames were soon overcome, but not before damage to the extent of between .E2OO and £3OO had been done. Fortu- nately, the fire was prevented from spreading to the mills, the efforts of the firemen being directed to confining it to the drying room only. None of the hands will be thrown out of employment, and the loss is covered by insurance. PRESENTATION TO A CURATE!, AT WARRINGTON A token of respect in which the Rev. J. E. Hand is held by the congregation and friends iitteliding the Bank-street Mission was afforded him on Sun- day afternoon, when, upon his severence from the work of the mission, he was presented with a beauti- fully illuminated album, which had been subscribed for by the teachers and scholars attending the Sun- day school. The presentation was made by Mr. Taurance, who spoke of the good work Mr. Hand had performed during his ministry in Warrington,, and said that he was universally i:espected by his congregation. The Rector, the Rev. F. W. Willis. also spoke in eulogistic terms of Mr. Hand's work. Mr. Hand, in reply, expressed his thankfulness to the friends at the mission. The album, which is very handsomely and elaborately bound, bore a suitable inscription.
THE-PROTECTION OF CHILDREN.

An application of a rather unusual nature was made to the Warrington magistrates at their sit- tings on Saturday and Monday. On the former day a man named William Douglas asked the Bench for a license for his boy, entitling him to perform at the Circus,in Sankey-st. He had been informed that the lad (who had been performing during the week) was under age; he would be seven next birthday. He was an acrobat.—The Clerk said it was neces- sary before the magistrates could grant a license for a medical man to examine the boy, see the nature of the performance, and certify whether it would be prejudicial .to his health. It would also be necessary for the boy to appear before the Bench. On Monday, Mr. Gibbs, the proprietor of the Circus, prOduced a certificate from Dr. Williams showing that there was nothing in the performance likely to prejudice the lad's healtk, either at present or in future. The Magistrate's Clerk said that the police had made inquiries, and found that the children were well attended to and enjoyed the perform- ance.—The Bench granted the required permission, intimating that it applied to performances in War- rington only. THE LADY WHISTLER AT THE PUBLIC HALL. The appearance of Mrs. Shaw, the celebrated society whistler, and Mr. T. A. Barrett's Opera Com- pany drew to the Public Hall a crowded audience on Monday evening. Not only were the seats com- pletely filled but all the standing room was monopo- lised. The entertainment was worthy of the gathering, for rarely has a Warrington audience been better entertained and amused than on Monday evening. The whistling of Mrs. Shaw was the sur- prise and wonder of those who heard it for the first time. The notes of this lady whistler are of the most melodiout description,and so full and resonant that they could be distinctly heard in every corner of the hall. They have been compared to those of 'various wind instruments, but perhaps they most , nearly resemble the carollings of the most noted of English singing birds. All the solos of Mrs. Shaw elicited hearsy encores, which werefreely responded to by the lady. All the other items in a long and admirably arranged programme also won the unmis- takeable approval of the audience. The Opera hoir was all ,that could be desired, while the liumerons ,performances of Mr. Lester Barrett at times simply:"raieed the audience to an uncon- trollable pitchofslaughter and applause.. I Suicrns: or A PLATMAN* AT SAN:kit 13Ritooks. On Monday. Mi. S. Brighouse, coroner for South- ' west Lancashire, held an inquest at the Black Horse, Sankey Bridges; on view of the body of Samuel Griffiths, a flatman, who hanged himself in theyard attached to his residence on Saturday.— Evidence of -identification was given ;by the widow, Alice Griffiths, who said that berlusband was 76 years of ago, and had lived with her at Sloop-fold. He had been poorly for about twelve weeks, and Dr. Joseph had been attending him. He had a very bad arm, which gave him a great deal of pain. For the past fortnight the pain had been so intense that deceased scarcely knew what he-was doing. About twenty minutes to six on Saturday eveningsleceased went out into the backyard. A few minutes later I witness, feeling anxious, followed with a lighted I candle, and saw him, as she supposed, standing in front of the closet door. She said " What are you doing there ?" Getting no reply she instinctively , felt that something dreadful had happened, and it so unnerved her that she dropped the candle, and how she reached the house she could not remember. --Joseph Lightfoot, a neighbour, said that the deceased's grand-daughter came running into his house on Saturday evening saying "Oh, Mr. Light- foot, grandfather has cut his throat." He went across the yard and saw the body of the deceased suspended by a rope near the closet door. The rope was reeved through the carving of the post and fastened round the neck of the deceased. The feet of the deceased were nearly touching the ground.' Witness cut the body down and carried it into the house. Deceased had been a great sufferer with his, arm.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that' deceased committed suicide whilst temporarily insane. WATcn NIGIIT SERVICE AT 1Y YCLIFFE CHURCH. On Tuesday night a. watch-night service was con- ducted at Wycliffe Church, Bewsoy-et., by the pas- tor, the Rev. John Yonge, assisted by the Rev. Edward Moore. The Her. E. Moore delivered a short address, and observed that the year fast pass- ing away had been to some a fulfillment of joy and long 'cherished hopes and of prosperity, but in the case of others how different it had been ! There were homes that were poorer, places that were vacant at the fireside, and hearts that were sad, and there were those who sighed "for the voice that is still.". The causes of happiness, Mr. Moore pointed out, eOsre in themselves, and there might still be happiness in the heart dospite all the changes of life. Might the new year upon which they were shortly to enter be a year of greater knowledge and •of trust in God and His truth. The Rev. J. Yonge said they knew the new year was coming, but let them be as distinctly certain of the greater truth, the truth more necessary for them to comprehend, "Behold, the Bridegroom cometh." It was simply impossible for a man, even through the long years of a long life on this earth, to avoid the meeting with his God. He might hear God calling , him as Adam did in the garden; nnd as Adam did, so might ; the man do, hide himself from God who sought him. None of them, even thole who tried most to live the Christian life, realized as it was becoming they should realize their personal accountability. Though the past year had been spent in forgetful- ness, in sin, and in evil, the Lord would have mercy upon them, and abundantly pardon if they would' only turn to Him. The last moments of the old and the first of the new year were spent in silent prayer, after which Mr. Yonge wished all "a happy new year." A hymn was sung and the Service us brought to a conclusion,
